title: [HashiCorp] From insight to action: improving infrastructure risk posture with Terraform and Concert
summary: Advances in AI are accelerating vulnerability discovery, uncovering previously unknown weaknesses and complex attack paths. Anthropic’s Claude Mythos cyber reasoning marked a major shift in the vulnerability landscape, demonstrating how frontier AI can identify vulnerabilities that have persisted through traditional testing and expert review. As discovery becomes faster and more sophisticated, organizations will face an even greater volume of findings to assess and prioritize. But finding more vulnerabilities is only the first step. To meaningfully reduce risk, teams need a way to determine which vulnerabilities matter most and a repeatable way to take action to address them. For many organizations, that path from detection to resolution remains fragmented. Disconnected workflows, manual handoffs, and complex infrastructure environments make it difficult to understand what is affected, whether a vulnerability can actually be exploited, and what changes are needed to resolve it. Until teams can turn those insights into action, vulnerabilities remain unresolved and organizations remain exposed. Improving infrastructure risk posture requires connecting vulnerability intelligence with the infrastructure context and governed workflows needed to act. In this blog, we’ll explore how Terraform and IBM Concert help organizations move from insight to action, connecting vulnerability intelligence, infrastructure context, and policy-driven governance as part of IBM’s infrastructure lifecycle management solution. The foundation for infrastructure context and governed action Before organizations can respond consistently to changing requirements, emerging vulnerabilities, or new operational needs, they need a trusted and repeatable way to make infrastructure changes. Without a common workflow for planning, reviewing, and applying these changes, organizations can struggle to translate decisions into safe, consistent action at scale. IBM Terraform has long served as the trusted foundation for defining, provisioning, and managing infrastructure as code throughout its lifecycle. By standardizing infrastructure changes through repeatable workflows, Terraform helps organizations establish a consistent operating model across increasingly complex hybrid cloud environments. At the core of Terraform’s value is the infrastructure context and governed execution it provides. Terraform configuration and state give teams a shared understanding of the infrastructure they manage, while capabilities like Infragraph extend that context into a shared substrate across IBM’s infrastructure portfolio. Accurate, timely context helps teams and agents understand what infrastructure exists, how resources are connected, and where changes may have downstream impact. Equally as important, Terraform provides the governed execution layer for acting on that context. Organizations can codify security, compliance, and operational requirements with policy as code, evaluate proposed changes against those requirements, and embed approvals and controls directly into their infrastructure workflows. Together, infrastructure context and policy-driven governance provide the foundation for controlled action at scale. These workflows become especially powerful when paired with vulnerability intelligence, creating a throughline from vulnerability discovery and prioritization to safe remediation. From vulnerability discovery to prioritized remediation As vulnerability discovery accelerates, teams are under increasing pressure to separate the findings that matter most from the noise and act before exposure turns into impact. The challenge is not simply finding more vulnerabilities, but understanding which ones can actually be exploited and determining what needs to be addressed first. IBM Concert Protect helps teams make that distinction, moving from discovery to evidence-based prioritization: Discover: IBM plans to bring Anthropic’s Claude Mythos cyber reasoning into IBM Concert Protect, extending discovery to previously unknown vulnerabilities, including weaknesses without existing signatures or CVE records. Mythos-powered findings are planned to enter Concert Protect alongside traditional scanner results, helping organizations expand what they can uncover without creating another disconnected source of findings. Validate: With capabilities such as Concert’s proof of exploitability, teams can determine which findings represent real-world exposure. Rather than relying solely on severity scores or exploitability predictions, the capability continuously correlates application, infrastructure, runtime, identity, network and business context to validate whether a vulnerability can actually be exploited within a customer’s environment. Remediate: Once teams understand what needs to be addressed, integrations with Terraform provide a governed path for making the required infrastructure changes. Teams can use established Terraform workflows to plan changes, evaluate them against policy, and execute them consistently across environments. The real value comes from connecting these stages into a unified, consistent vulnerability management workflow. This helps organizations mitigate infrastructure risk more effectively by uncovering more vulnerabilities, validating what matters, and taking action safely at scale. Learn more Together, Terraform and IBM Concert help organizations connect vulnerability discovery and prioritization with the infrastructure context and governed workflows needed to act, creating a more complete approach to improving risk posture across the infrastructure lifecycle. To learn more, join IBM and HashiCorp experts for Rethinking enterprise risk in the AI world on November 19, 2026 at 11 a.m. EST. The 45-minute webinar will explore how advances in AI, including Anthropic’s Claude Mythos, are reshaping vulnerability discovery, how proof of exploitability can help teams determine which risks matter most, and how Terraform can help translate prioritized findings into controlled infrastructure changes. title: [CNCF] Is your OpenTelemetry pipeline becoming a performance bottleneck?
summary: At Cloud Native Days Austria 2026, I presented a talk called How to Defeat OTel’s Silent Killer: The Performance Overhead, exploring a problem that is easy to overlook when building observability pipelines: the cost of collecting telemetry itself. OpenTelemetry has become a cornerstone of cloud-native observability, providing standardized APIs, SDKs, and tooling for generating, collecting, processing, and exporting metrics, logs, and traces. However, instrumentation and telemetry processing are not free. Every span created, attribute attached, and batch exported consumes resources. As applications scale, poorly configured telemetry pipelines can introduce significant CPU usage, memory pressure, network traffic, and storage costs. In some cases, the infrastructure responsible for observing a system can become a performance problem of its own. The good news is that much of this overhead can be understood, measured, and reduced without sacrificing the visibility engineers depend on. Where does OpenTelemetry overhead come from? When discussing OpenTelemetry performance, we often focus on the application SDK. However, the cost extends beyond instrumentation. The entire telemetry pipeline contributes to resource consumption, from generating spans and collecting metrics to processing, exporting, and storing data. Instrumentation overhead is also workload-dependent. Two applications using the same instrumentation libraries can experience very different results depending on request throughput, attribute volume, runtime behavior, and the number of spans generated per request. This is why relying on a single overhead percentage can be misleading. Instead, we should examine CPU consumption, memory usage, application latency, telemetry volume, and the behavior of the Collector under load. There is also an important trade-off between application safety and telemetry completeness. When a pipeline becomes overloaded, backpressure and memory safeguards can protect the application and OpenTelemetry Collector, but they may also lead to rejected or dropped telemetry. The objective is not simply to minimize resource consumption. It is to maintain useful observability while keeping its operational cost predictable. Investigating the Collector: five common configuration problems For my demonstration, I used Telemetrygen, an OpenTelemetry utility that generates synthetic telemetry, to investigate how Collector configuration affects resource consumption. The investigation focused on five common sources of unnecessary overhead. 1. Inefficient batching Exporting small amounts of telemetry frequently can increase serialization work, export requests, and network overhead. The OpenTelemetry Collector groups telemetry inside the exporter’s sending queue before transmitting it downstream, helping amortize this work across larger payloads. (Note: Historically, this was handled by a standalone batch processor, which is now deprecated in favor of built-in exporter batching). However, batching parameters should reflect the actual workload. Larger batches are not automatically better: they can increase buffering requirements and affect export latency. exporters: otlp_grpc: endpoint: "otel-backend:4317" sending_queue: enabled: true sizer: items queue_size: 100000 batch: enabled: true min_size: 8192 flush_timeout: 200ms Configuring batch inside an exporter’s sending_queue groups spans, metrics, or logs before forwarding them downstream, improving compression efficiency and durability while reducing export overhead. Batches are sent when a configured size threshold is reached or a timeout expires. In this example, min_size: 8192 triggers an export when the batch reaches 8,192 items, while flush_timeout: 200ms triggers an export regardless of batch size. Once batching is enabled, these values are the Collector’s documented defaults, not universal performance recommendations. (Note: Because unbatched requests enter the queue first in this architecture, this example switches sizer from the default requests to items with a queue_size of 100000 to prevent smaller, unbatched bursts from overflowing the queue). The important point is to measure how batching affects resource consumption and throughput rather than relying on example configurations. 2. Unnecessary resource attributes Resource attributes provide valuable context about the systems producing telemetry. But collecting and forwarding attributes that nobody uses can increase payload sizes and downstream processing costs. For example, an application might need host.name, host.arch, and os.type for troubleshooting, but not detailed hardware information such as host.cpu.model.name or host.cpu.cache.l2.size. The OpenTelemetry Collector’s resource detection processor allows engineers to configure which system attributes are collected. Disabling unnecessary attributes can reduce telemetry volume and processing overhead, although the impact on storage and cardinality depends on the backend. A practical example: Keep the hostname and operating system type, but disable CPU model and cache metadata when those details are not needed for troubleshooting. 3. Aggressive receiver polling Infrastructure receivers collect metrics at configured intervals, often independently of application traffic. Polling host metrics, container statistics, databases, and network services every few seconds creates continuous work even when applications are relatively idle. Increasing collection intervals from 10 to 30 seconds, where operational requirements permit, can reduce collection frequency and associated overhead. This introduces a trade-off: lower polling frequency means less temporal resolution. The appropriate interval depends on how quickly a metric changes and how it is used for troubleshooting or alerting. 4. Exporting every trace Not every successful request needs to produce a trace that is retained. Exporting all traces can consume significant bandwidth, Collector resources, and backend capacity, particularly in high-throughput applications. Sampling provides a way to control this volume. Head-based sampling makes decisions early, reducing downstream work. Tail-based sampling makes decisions after observing more of a trace, enabling policies that retain errors or other diagnostically interesting requests. These policies retain traces with an error status and probabilistically sample 5% of traces, including potentially some additional error traces. However, tail sampling is not free. It requires buffering trace data until a decision can be made, introducing additional memory and processing overhead. Choosing a sampling strategy means balancing cost, diagnostic value, and the resources needed to make sampling decisions. 5. Memory safeguards applied too late The OpenTelemetry Collector includes a memory_limiter processor to help manage memory pressure. Processor ordering matters. When enrichment and transformation processors run before memory limiting, the Collector may perform additional work on telemetry that is subsequently refused under memory pressure. Memory limiting is a protective mechanism rather than a performance optimization in itself. Its purpose is to improve stability under pressure, not necessarily to reduce CPU consumption during normal operation. Placing the memory limiter early in the pipeline helps apply safeguards before more expensive processing. It is important to understand that the memory limiter is not a substitute for appropriate resource limits or capacity planning. It can refuse incoming data when memory pressure becomes excessive, and receivers must handle this behavior correctly to avoid unnecessary telemetry loss. From local experiments to production architecture Optimizing a single Collector is only part of the solution. In Kubernetes, telemetry workloads can fluctuate significantly as applications scale, deployments change, and traffic increases. A Collector configuration that performs well under synthetic load may behave differently in production. Here are some architectural practices that can help address these challenges. Separate collection from centralized processing. A two-tier architecture can use lightweight edge Collectors for local collection and gateway Collectors for more expensive processing. This allows different parts of the pipeline to scale according to their workloads. Control telemetry volume early. Filtering unnecessary attributes, removing unneeded data, and avoiding excessive cardinality can reduce the amount of information processed and transferred downstream. These decisions should preserve the context required for debugging and correlation. Plan for memory pressure and backend outages. Kubernetes memory limits, Collector memory safeguards, bounded queues, and retry mechanisms serve different purposes. Persistent queues can improve resilience during temporary backend failures, but they still require capacity planning and cannot guarantee delivery under every failure scenario. Scale with signal-specific requirements in mind. Horizontal scaling can increase throughput, but stateful processing requires additional consideration. Tail sampling, for example, generally requires spans belonging to the same trace to reach the same processing instance. These architectural decisions are just as important as tuning individual processors. Don’t forget the instrumentation One of the most effective optimizations happens before telemetry reaches the Collector. Instrumentation should answer meaningful operational questions rather than collect everything simply because it is possible. Excessive spans, high-cardinality attributes, and unnecessary instrumentation can increase resource consumption throughout the entire pipeline. For metrics, attributes containing unbounded values such as unique request IDs can create large numbers of distinct time series. For traces and logs, excessive attributes and events increase payload sizes and may affect backend processing or indexing costs. Why I chose Telemetrygen for my demo When preparing my performance investigation, I initially considered using the official OpenTelemetry Astronomy Shop. While it is an excellent environment for exploring instrumentation across microservices, its multiple applications, databases, and supporting services introduce additional CPU and memory consumption. For this experiment, I wanted to isolate the Collector’s performance overhead without the background noise of a complete application environment. Instead, I chose Telemetrygen, a lightweight utility for generating synthetic traces, metrics, and logs at controlled rates. In my OpenTelemetry performance overhead demo, I used synthetic telemetry to investigate how Collector configuration affects resource consumption. The demonstration walks through common inefficiencies, including missing batching, unnecessary resource attributes, aggressive receiver polling, excessive trace export, and memory limiter placement, showing how targeted configuration changes can improve pipeline efficiency. This approach helped isolate Collector behavior, but it is only one part of the performance picture. For understanding instrumentation overhead inside real applications, a complete environment such as Astronomy Shop remains valuable. Exploring instrumentation further Reducing overhead starts with understanding what telemetry an application generates and why. The official OpenTelemetry instrumentation documentation introduces automatic and manual instrumentation, while the sampling documentation explains how to control trace volume. These are useful starting points for reviewing instrumentation decisions before optimizing the Collector itself. For engineers interested in investigating performance further, the OpenTelemetry Collector documentation covers pipeline configuration and processing. The OpenTelemetry community is also a good place to discuss performance challenges. The Collector SIG focuses on Collector architecture, performance, and configuration, with discussions taking place in the #otel-collector channel on CNCF Slack. For questions about instrumentation overhead in a specific programming language, the corresponding language SIG is a better starting point. The OpenTelemetry community page provides information about SIGs, public meetings, and how to get involved. Making performance part of observability design OpenTelemetry overhead is not a single problem with a single configuration fix. It is the combined effect of instrumentation decisions, data volume, processor configuration, export behavior, and infrastructure architecture. The most useful lesson from this investigation is that observability pipelines should be measured and optimized like any other production system. Start with controlled benchmarks. Understand where resources are consumed. Introduce configuration changes individually, and evaluate their impact on CPU, memory, latency, throughput, and telemetry loss. Most importantly, treat example configurations as starting points rather than production-ready defaults. OpenTelemetry gives us the tools to understand complex distributed systems. With thoughtful instrumentation, careful pipeline configuration, and appropriate scaling strategies, we can ensure that collecting this information does not become an unnecessary burden on the systems we are trying to observe.

title: [Netflix] Engineering AI Discover
summary: The challenges and decisions behind AI Discover’s intelligence layerBy Varun Khaitan, Peng Ren, Gary Tang, Itay Teller, Atif Faheem, Nipun Kumar, Donnie DeBoer, Eduardo Lundgren, Matteo Rinaldi, Raghav BakshiWe recently introduced AI Discover, a new tab in our TV app where a small group of members can try new ways to find something to watch. For years, our recommendations have worked in the background, inferring what a member might enjoy from their viewing history. AI Discover moves from that silent ranking toward steerable discovery. A member picks a theme, say “Quick Watches,” and gets a row of matching titles, a short note on why they fit and a few narrower themes to try next. From there, they can keep narrowing, head somewhere new or tune what they see.Building AI Discover raised a question many teams will recognize: how do you deliver a better member experience with generative AI on TV without sacrificing speed, reliability or safety? Our answer is a new intelligence layer, the agent harness behind AI Discover. For each request, it decides how to combine LLMs with our recommendation systems. It builds on years of work understanding what members enjoy, and on our recent work applying LLMs to recommendations and generative experiences. The layer itself plans each request, runs it across those systems, serves the result and evaluates it offline.This post covers the challenges we designed for and the key decisions we made along the way.Why an intelligence layer?Every Netflix page combines recommendations with rules. We pick titles a member may enjoy, and eligibility, maturity and safety rules decide what can appear. An experience built on LLMs needs the same rules, plus code that decides when to call an LLM and how to handle its output. That code is called an agent harness, and it’s the core of our intelligence layer.The simplest implementation hands the entire request to an LLM and lets it pick the titles, write the labels and decide what happens next. However, that leaves us relying on probabilistic output where we need governed results, because every turn in AI Discover ends on a screen in someone’s living room. At our scale, even rare failures happen many times a day. A member sees every slow call, unavailable title or off-brand line. Seven challenges shaped our design:Fitting LLMs into a product and architecture designed without them. Traditional recommenders rank titles based on past behavior. LLMs can do more: understand what a member is asking for and plan how to respond. Our existing experience would leave most of that unused.Keeping recommendations grounded. Every pick must be a real, available title from our changing catalog. Retrieval and rankers work in tandem with LLMs to choose titles that fit the member’s taste and intent.Working with slow, unpredictable LLMs. LLM calls are the slowest and most expensive part of the system. Tail latencies can spike, and the output may not be what you asked for. So we use LLMs selectively, treat what they return as untrusted input and test performance and quality before anything ships.Adapting to fast-changing models, tools and prompts. Modeling and engineering solutions keep evolving, so the product can’t depend on any single model, tool or prompt.Building for TV. Typing on a TV is hard, so members rely on the remote, and the app should respond to every press right away on widely varying hardware. TV apps also update slowly, so changes have to ship without an app release. A typical TV request returns in moments, while multi-step generation can take several seconds.Holding a safety and reliability bar at scale. Members always get a page, even when an LLM call fails or yields poor results. Their choices and our content standards hold on every request, and when something breaks, structured records show why.Learning from what members say alongside what we already know. Recommendations have always learned from viewing behavior. AI Discover also lets members tell us what they want, and that has to shape what they see next.System ArchitectureWhen a member picks a theme, the TV app sends the request to the Page Server, which builds pages for all Netflix apps and hands the request asynchronously to the intelligence layer. At a high level, this new layer has two components: a controller and an executor.The controller decides what to run. It gathers the context needed for each request, including real-time signals such as the time of day. It then settles on a plan, either an established one or a new one drafted by its planner, validates it and retrieves only the member details that this plan requires from Memory Hub, our per-member memory store. These details may include member taste summaries generated by MemberLLM, our in-house language model for personalized recommendations, or feedback shared by the member. We talk more about Memory Hub and member taste summaries later.A plan is a graph of approved steps, each running a capability. A capability is a named unit of work that can have multiple versions and belongs to a family such as retrieval, ranking, generation or packaging. It declares its inputs and outputs, the context it may see and what happens if it fails.Capability declarations make a plan verifiable. Before execution, the controller validates the graph: every step is approved, every input has a producer, nothing loops and the plan ends in exactly one page. Afterward, the controller checks the result before it’s served.The executor runs the plan. Steps pass typed outputs to each other through the declared contracts, so each receives exactly what it asked for. Independent steps run in parallel, each with its own deadline and appropriate fallback behaviors. Some steps are optimized LLM calls with one task each, such as writing row titles or suggesting next themes, and they act only within the validated plan. Checks before the run and contracts during it give us governed execution, where every action stays within limits set in code.Both parts write to the request records, the traces we use offline to evaluate and improve the system.System Architecture DiagramKey DecisionsEach challenge led to one decision. Here’s what we chose and what it bought us.1. Design the product and architecture around LLMsWe reimagined the experience around LLMs. The easier path would have been to drop them in as rankers, keep today’s latency budgets and precompute where necessary. AI Discover is built on a back-and-forth around themes a member can steer, which gives LLMs work only they can do: generating themes, explaining rows, summarizing taste and helping choose the titles that fit the member and the moment. Members pick themes with the remote, so they never have to type. On the TV, those themes and explanations get their own native UI elements. Behind the screen, LLMs can draft plans, and asynchronous serving gives multi-step agentic orchestration the time it needs.This opens up experiences our traditional stack couldn’t support on its own.2. Make existing systems composableKeeping recommendations grounded meant building on the systems that already know our catalog and members. Most capabilities wrap complex, proven Netflix systems such as search, large-scale ranking and catalog metadata access. Some of them may run their own agents in the future.Reshaping them took careful work, because agentic orchestration challenges many long-standing assumptions of distributed systems. A capability now has to work in combinations no one designed, for a caller that chooses to call it at runtime. Each one needs a clear purpose and a semantic interface, and shaping it means deciding how much to combine into a single step and how much to leave to the planner. Too fine, and the planner has more ways to go wrong; too coarse, and it loses room to compose richer plans.In return, the planner gets building blocks it can mix in new ways, and connecting services takes far less manual wiring. Because plans can only use these blocks, even one drafted on the fly stays grounded in our catalog and member taste.3. Plan first, then executeTo contain LLM latency and errors, we plan every request before anything runs. The familiar way to let an agent use tools is a loop: reason, call a tool, read the result, reason again. It’s flexible, but you can’t tell up front how many steps it will take or whether it has gone down a wrong path. In agent terms, ours is a plan-and-execute agent: an LLM can propose the path, but code decides whether it runs.Plans come from two places: established plans we’ve already tested, and plans an LLM drafts on the fly. A router we control decides which one is served. Either way, the plan passes the same checks before it runs. If the planner is slow or its plan fails a check, we fall back to a tested plan.This allows for adaptive planning. The planner can find new ways to serve a request, and we can balance cost, latency and quality for each task, from a lean single-call plan to a richer multi-step one.4. Stay model and capability agnosticThe best model or capability for a task today may be second-best, or overkill, in a few months, so we built the system to switch between them. We assign each task to the model or capability version that fits it. Today that’s a per-task setting we can override live. Only some steps in a request use an LLM.That only works if switching is easy. All the LLMs we use sit behind one common interface. Before we switch, each candidate is scored on the same tasks by automated checks and LLM judges, so every swap is a measured change.Much of the system’s behavior lives in server-side prompts and configuration, so we can swap models, tools and capabilities without new code or a TV app release.Upgrades get cheap and experiments get easy. Moving to a better model, ranker or retrieval system is a plan or setting change, not a migration, so each component can keep improving without a large investment.5. Make page generation asynchronousInference keeps getting faster, but member expectations rise just as quickly: richer responses, more context and more of the page shaped by LLMs. The line between what feels instant and what’s worth waiting for will keep shifting, so we built the asynchronous path as a first-class way of serving.Most of a TV app is synchronous: press a button, get a page. Generative work breaks that pattern. Holding one request open for many seconds across services would tie up too many threads. So requests that involve generation are asynchronous. The press returns right away with an acknowledgement, and the TV switches to a thinking state that explains what’s being prepared. Meanwhile, the executor runs the plan in the background. When the result is ready, the server notifies the TV, which then fetches it.Slow generation no longer slows anything else. The serving path stays healthy however long a turn takes, and every press still gets immediate feedback on screen.Async Sequence Diagram6. Enforce safety in codeSome rules must hold no matter what an LLM writes: content and maturity standards, what each step can access, and what a member has asked us not to show them. Putting those rules in a prompt makes them probabilistic, so we enforce them in code. Generated text is cleaned up before it reaches the screen. The planner sees a stripped-down request, and member details are limited to what the validated plan needs.For example, the planner decides which inputs each step needs, such as the profile’s maturity rating for retrieval. Instead of writing parameter values directly, it uses placeholders. After the plan passes validation, the controller fills them with values from the request, matched by declared type. This also protects against prompt injection.Each request also leaves a structured record: the plan, each step and its outcome, and which rules applied. When a page misses, we can tell whether the plan, the data, a rule or the model was at fault. The same records feed our offline evaluation and replay.Together, these rules and records let an experiment ship at the same safety and privacy bar as the rest of the product.7. Remember what members tell usA taste summary is a short profile of what a member enjoys, such as favorite genres, tone and recurring themes. MemberLLM generates it ahead of time from the member’s viewing history, which keeps that LLM work off the request path. It helps us further personalize their page, and steps that write themes and explanations receive it as context, so their wording reflects the member. We’ll cover MemberLLM in more detail in an upcoming post.In AI Discover, members can also tune their recommendations and tell us directly what they want. Those choices apply right away and carry across visits, and they give us a new signal alongside what we already know about their taste. This is a first step toward remembering more about each member, from their preferences to the habits that show up over time and the corners of the catalog they like to explore. We keep it all in Memory Hub, our persistent, low-latency memory store, next to their taste summaries, and we can add new kinds of memory as we need them. We apply these memories to later requests where they’re relevant, together with real-time context.The member holds the remoteIn this version, members interact by selecting themes and using tuning options such as “don’t recommend.” There’s no free-text input or open-ended chat. That keeps the LLM’s job narrow by design.The usual protections still apply. Profile settings and our safety and privacy policies hold here as everywhere else.Generated text was tested before launch. We ran safety evaluations on theme labels, row titles and explanations to make sure they meet our standards.What’s nextIt would have been faster to let an LLM do everything and stop there. The intelligence layer gave us an AI-native product, grounded building blocks, adaptive planning, quicker experimentation, asynchronous generation, governed execution and agent memory for tunable personalization. While AI Discover is its first experience, we designed it with more in mind.We’ve organized our efforts to answer two questions:How much do members want to shape their recommendations? Whether they’d rather steer or lean back, and how much, which kinds of themes help, and how we should blend what members tell us with our existing personalization systems.What tradeoffs does this technology bring? How cost and latency hold up in production as we ramp traffic, how long members will wait for generated results, and whether errors came from the model, the harness or our existing systems. Multi-turn sessions also need different evaluation and observability than single requests.Longer term, our goal is a system that improves itself, starting from the record each request leaves behind. Today we replay past requests against a new prompt, model or rule to see what changes, and we judge each change with automated checks, LLM judges and human evaluations. Eventually, we want the system to propose improvements, test them safely and keep only what proves better, within our privacy and data-use policies. As LLMs improve, more of the work may move into them, and the intelligence layer lets us move that line deliberately.This is part of a bigger shift. Recommendation systems have long learned quietly from what members watch and answered with ranked rows. LLMs let them listen and respond, and members may increasingly expect that. We’ll keep exploring what that means for discovery on Netflix.AcknowledgementsWe would like to thank Adi Suresh, Akash Katipally, Allan Johns, Becks Wood, Bhargav Mangipudi, Carrie Santiago, Chris Martin, Claire Campbell, Corey Waldin, Dana Sittler, Daneo Zhang, David Leen, Devon Bryant, Dharamendra Kumar, Dharini Chandrasekaran, Ebony Turner, Federico Roa, Gianfranco Cuoco, Guru Tahasildar, Haley Clanton, Haresh Chudgar, Ivan Provalov, James Schultz, JingXu Yang, Josie Shaw, Kamelia Aryafar, Kate Cummings, Kathleen Garrity, Kelley Robinson, Kevin Du, Kevin O’Connor, Kyla Moore, Kyle Lind, Laura Matsuura, Leah Cusella, Lingyi Liu, Lingyong Wang, Mallory Walkup, Matthew Pereira, Michael Galassi, Minsu Jang, Moumita Bhattacharya, Paran Jain, Paul Lee, Qusai Al-Rabadi, Scarlet Chen, Sergi Perez, Sriram Rao, Stephen Shaw, Sura Elamurugu, Varad Pathak, Yesu Feng, Zainab Mahar Mir, and Zhongli Cheng for their contributions to this work.Engineering AI Discover was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Kubernetes] Scheduling the removal of the kube-proxy IPVS backend
summary: The ipvs backend for kube-proxy was an experiment in providing a service proxy implementation with better performance than the iptables backend. While it succeeded in that goal, the kernel IPVS API has turned out to be a bad match for the Kubernetes Services API, and the ipvs backend was never able to implement all of the edge cases of Kubernetes Service functionality correctly. In Kubernetes 1.29, the project introduced the nftables backend for kube-proxy, which became GA in 1.33. Part of the plan behind adding the nftables backend was the idea that it would eventually replace both the iptables and ipvs backends. Because the ipvs backend in particular is complex, not 100% feature complete, and architecturally quite different from the other two backends (and thus more work to maintain), Kubernetes SIG Network decided to officially deprecate it as of Kubernetes 1.35. Although it currently remains available in kube-proxy (with a warning about its deprecation), we (Kubernetes SIG Network) now plan to remove it in Kubernetes 1.40. All ipvs users should therefore be planning to migrate to either the nftables or iptables backends. Why was the ipvs backend written?The ipvs backend was originally designed to fix two different kinds of performance problems in the iptables backend: First, iptables had problems with data plane latency (the speed at which clients could establish new connections to services), because kube-proxy would write a separate iptables rule to match each service IP, so every new connection would need to be matched against a long series of rules that was O(n) in the number of services in the cluster. Second, it had an even larger problem with control plane latency (the speed at which kube-proxy could process changes to services and endpoints and update the data plane rules), because kube-proxy would rewrite the entire iptables ruleset every time any service or endpoint changed. While the list of rules itself was only O(n) in the total number of endpoints, the amount of time, RAM, and CPU that it took to process the updated ruleset grew faster than that. In very large clusters, kube-proxy would use 100% of one CPU all the time just to process iptables updates. (In fact, the control plane scaling problem was bad enough that for most users it was not even possible to grow the cluster to the size where the data plane scaling problem became noticeable.) The ipvs backend solved both of these scaling problems. The data plane problem was solved mostly automatically, because the kernel IPVS subsystem uses hash tables rather than linear lookup. The control-plane problem was solved by not rewriting the entire ruleset on every update. (The kernel IPVS API doesn’t have a way of doing batch updates anyway, so this was essentially forced.) Why is the ipvs backend now being deprecated?Almost from the start, the ipvs backend also had problems. The first version didn’t have 100% compatibility with the iptables backend, but it was assumed that this would be fixed over time. Unfortunately, the original authors moved on to other things outside the Kubernetes ecosystem (as inevitably sometimes happens in open source), and it took a while to find new people interested in maintaining the code. Meanwhile, as people began using the ipvs backend in larger and larger clusters, its own scaling problems started to emerge. In particular, the lack of batch update operations in the IPVS API meant that while the ipvs backend was faster than iptables when making a few small changes, it was potentially slower when making a large number of changes at once. And because the IPVS API is fairly limited in what it can do, kube-proxy's ipvs backend needed to fall back to using iptables to implement various features of Kubernetes Services beyond basic "load balancing", making it run into some of the same scaling problems the iptables backend has. While the ipvs backend tried to mitigate this by using ipset for some of its rules, this again ran into the problem of not having a batch update API. Additionally, the fact that the ipvs backend uses iptables means that it has the same long-term support problem as the iptables backend: Red Hat's plan to remove the iptables API entirely from Red Hat Enterprise Linux means the ipvs kube-proxy backend will also no longer be available to Kubernetes users on RHEL. What about IPVS schedulers?Beyond performance, the other reason some users were excited about the ipvs backend was the ability to pick from among various IPVS "schedulers" for distributing traffic to endpoints, rather than relying on the simple random selection used by iptables (and nftables). Unfortunately, the way IPVS is used by kube-proxy prevents it from being able to use most of the IPVS schedulers in a useful way. The problem is that kube-proxy is a distributed service that runs on all nodes in the cluster, but the kube-proxy processes on different nodes do not share their IPVS scheduler state, so each node picks endpoints without knowing what is happening with clients on any other node. Even the schedulers that are designed to work in a distributed way generally don't work better than random selection in the context of kube-proxy. For example, the mh scheduler uses Maglev Hashing to select endpoints, which theoretically allows for extremely efficient distributed load balancing. But that efficiency is only in the context of a specific sort of two-layer load-balancer design, and kube-proxy does not have the right architecture to be able to act as either of the two layers in that design. Switching away from ipvsSwitching to nftablesIf you are running Kubernetes 1.36 or later, and your nodes are running a Linux distribution with kernel 5.13 or later, and you use the ipvs proxy mode, then Kubernetes recommends switching to the nftables mode of kube-proxy. (Although the nftables backend is GA —and fully usable—as of Kubernetes 1.33, there have been some performance- and scaling-related fixes since then that that weren't backported to releases earlier than 1.36.) The nftables backend is fully supported, feature-complete, and even has very slightly better performance than ipvs: (Taller bars represent longer latency. The "p50" group is the average connection establishment latency. Note that even the largest numbers in this graph are quite tiny; the point is not to claim that nftables is (noticeably) faster than ipvs, just to show that, unlike iptables, it's not slower.) Switching is as easy as changing the kube-proxy configuration and restarting kube-proxy. For example, in clusters deployed via kubeadm, change mode: ipvs to mode: nftables in the kube-proxy ConfigMap and then restart the kube-proxy pods, as described in the documentation on reconfiguring a kubeadm cluster. (If you are overriding other ipvs-specific kube-proxy configuration, you will also need to change those options to the corresponding nftables ones.) Switching to iptables: "It's Not As Slow As You Think!"If you can't switch to nftables, either because you are on an older version of Kubernetes, or because your cluster runs on an older Linux distribution that isn't new enough to support the nftables backend, you may be able to just switch to the iptables backend, which has improved greatly since the original creation of the ipvs backend in 2017: The generated ruleset has been optimized to remove redundant and irrelevant rules (#57461, #60306, #96959, #108251), reducing data plane latency. The code that generates the ruleset has been optimized to do fewer allocations, and to avoid unnecessarily recomputing the same information multiple times (#65755, #65902, #67948, #85617, #90103, #97238), reducing CPU and memory usage when resyncing. Rather than doing “check the current state of the rules, then update them to the new state”, iptables kube-proxy now does “assume the current state is correct, update to the new state based on that assumption, and only explicitly check the current state if that update fails”. This greatly improves the resyncing speed, because it turns out that even reading the iptables ruleset is extremely slow in large clusters (#81517, #110334, #114181). To the extent possible within the constraints of the iptables APIs, kube-proxy’s iptables backend now only updates iptables rules for services/endpoints that have changed since the last sync, rather than rewriting the entire ruleset every time (#110268 / KEP-3453). The net result of this is that the iptables backend of 2026, while still not as good as the ipvs backend, is at least much better than the iptables backend of 2017 was, and many people who found iptables unusable in the past would not have problems with it now. As with switching to nftables, switching to iptables is mostly just a matter of updating your kube-proxy configuration, although for technical reasons, in this case we recommend that you reboot each node after changing the kube-proxy configuration, rather than merely restarting kube-proxy. Learn more KEP-5495 gives the full timeline and plan for kube-proxy IPVS deprecation. The blog post "NFTables mode for kube-proxy" has more information about nftables mode and its performance relative to ipvs and iptables.

title: [Kubernetes] The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know
summary:
In Linux, cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources. Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers, ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other. With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into maintenance mode. Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25. Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy, a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation and modern resource-management features. Deprecation of cgroup v1Kubernetes has deprecated cgroup v1. Starting with Kubernetes v1.35, failCgroupV1 defaults to true, so the kubelet does not start on a cgroup v1 node by default. Administrators can temporarily set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration file, but removal will follow the Kubernetes deprecation policy. Further removal work is tracked in KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support. If you are still on a release older than v1.35, migrate every Linux node to cgroup v2 before upgrading, or plan to set the temporary failCgroupV1: false override. If you are already on v1.35 or later, confirm that every Linux node runs cgroup v2 (or that you intentionally keep the override). Under the default configuration, a remaining cgroup v1 node fails during kubelet startup. For kubeadm-managed clusters, Kubernetes v1.35 also makes this an earlier, stricter check. The SystemVerification preflight check, provided by k8s.io/system-validators, returns an error during kubeadm init, kubeadm join, and kubeadm upgrade when it detects cgroup v1 with kubelet v1.35 or later; with an older kubelet, the check remains a warning. See kubernetes/system-validators#1.12.1 release notes for details. The top FAQs cover three main areas: why to migrate, the benefits and drawbacks, and key points to keep in mind when using cgroup v2. Limitations of cgroup v1 and Improvements with cgroup v2The Linux kernel documentation describes both interfaces: cgroup v1 documentation cgroup v2 documentation Let's enumerate some known issues. active_file memory is not considered available memoryThe kubelet treats active_file memory as not reclaimable. For I/O-intensive workloads, a large page cache can therefore make the kubelet report memory pressure and evict Pods. This is a known kubelet issue (kubernetes/kubernetes#43916); migrating to cgroup v2 does not by itself change that calculation. The documented workaround is to set equal memory requests and limits for containers that perform intensive I/O, after measuring an appropriate value. Memory QoS updates in Kubernetes v1.36Memory QoS was introduced as an alpha feature in Kubernetes v1.22 and updated in v1.27. It remains alpha in v1.36, but now separates memory throttling from memory reservation and adds tiered memory protection: Memory QoS is available only on Linux nodes that use cgroup v2. It relies on the cgroup v2 memory controller: memory.high provides throttling, while memory.min and memory.low provide hard and soft protection when tiered reservation is enabled. cgroup v1 cannot provide this protection model. Enabling the MemoryQoS feature gate applies memory.high throttling to Burstable containers. The threshold is derived from the request, limit, and memoryThrottlingFactor (default 0.9). memoryReservationPolicy: None is the default. It does not write memory.min or memory.low. memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation maps Guaranteed Pod memory requests to memory.min (hard protection) and Burstable Pod requests to memory.low (soft protection). BestEffort Pods receive neither protection. The kubelet exposes Alpha metrics for the total memory.min and memory.low reservations on a node. Kernel 5.9 or later is recommended. On older kernels, memory.high reclaim can trigger a known livelock; from v1.36 the kubelet logs a warning when Memory QoS is enabled on an affected kernel. For example, to opt in to tiered protection: apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: KubeletConfiguration featureGates: MemoryQoS: true memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation memoryThrottlingFactor: 0.9 The overall Kubernetes recommendation is not to enable Alpha features in production; however, if you judge that memory QoS with tiered reservations is useful for your platform in production, make sure to test the configuration and account for hard-reserved memory before you enable the TieredReservation feature gate. See the Pod QoS documentation for the current mapping of Kubernetes QoS classes to cgroup v2 controls. Container-aware OOM handlingOn cgroup v2 nodes, the kubelet defaults singleProcessOOMKill to false. It therefore sets memory.oom.group for each container cgroup so that an OOM event kills all processes in that container together, rather than leaving a partially functioning multi-process container. Set singleProcessOOMKill: true only if you need the cgroup v1-compatible behavior where the kernel may kill one process at a time. See the KubeletConfiguration reference for this setting. This behavior is scoped to a container cgroup, not the whole Pod. Also, cgroup.kill is a separate administrative interface: writing 1 to it sends SIGKILL to every process in that cgroup and its descendants; it does not configure OOM behavior. The cgroup v2 memory controller additionally provides memory.events counters that monitoring systems and userspace OOM managers can observe. Rootless supportIn cgroup v1, delegating controllers to less privileged containers may be dangerous. Unlike cgroup v1, cgroup v2 officially supports delegation. Most implementations of rootless containers rely on systemd for delegating v2 controllers to non-root users. This delegation mechanism is separate from Kubernetes Pod user namespaces, which map container users to unprivileged host users. Pod user namespace support graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.36; check its filesystem, kernel, CRI runtime, and OCI runtime prerequisites before enabling it. What else? eBPF stories: In cgroup v1, device access controls are exposed through interface files. The cgroup v2 device controller has no interface files, and is implemented on top of cgroup BPF. Cilium attaches BPF cgroup programs for socket-based load balancing. Its default cgroup root is /run/cilium/cgroupv2. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) reports CPU, memory, and I/O contention at node, Pod, and container level. On supported clusters, the kubelet exposes PSI by default (KubeletPSI is stable and locked on). PSI requires cgroup v2, Linux 4.20 or later, CONFIG_PSI=y, and a kernel not booted with psi=0. The kubelet surfaces the data through the Summary API and /metrics/cadvisor. When migrating, update software that reads the cgroup filesystem directly. The migration guidance recommends cAdvisor v0.43.0 or later and lists compatible Java, Node.js, and automaxprocs versions. CPU weight conversion in newer OCI runtimescgroup v1 uses cpu.shares, whereas cgroup v2 uses cpu.weight. Newer OCI runtimes use an improved non-linear conversion that preserves the default priority and gives small CPU requests more usable granularity. The change is implemented in the OCI runtime rather than Kubernetes: it is available in crun v1.23 and runc v1.3.2. After upgrading a runtime, monitoring or policy tools that predict exact cpu.weight values may need updates. Read New Conversion from cgroup v1 CPU Shares to v2 CPU Weight for the formula, examples, and compatibility considerations. In-place resource updatesIn-place Pod vertical scaling graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.35. Kubernetes v1.36 then  (/blog/2026/04/30/kubernetes-v1-36-inplace-pod-level-resources-beta/) in-place vertical scaling for Pod-level resources by default, as a Beta feature. The kubelet coordinates changes between the Pod-level and container cgroups so that increases create headroom before container limits grow, while decreases constrain containers before shrinking the Pod-level boundary. Accurate aggregate enforcement for this v1.36 feature requires cgroup v2. Adopting cgroup version 2RequirementsHere's what you need to use cgroup v2 with Kubernetes. First up, you need to be using a version of Kubernetes with support for v2 cgroup management; that's been stable since Kubernetes v1.25 and all supported Kubernetes releases include this support. You need at least one Linux node; cgroup is a Linux-only concept Your OS install must run with cgroup v2 enabled The kernel version must be 5.8 or later (5.9 or later is recommended when using memory QoS) The container runtime must support cgroup v2. For example: containerd v1.4 or later supports cgroup v2; use containerd v2.0 or later for automatic cgroup-driver discovery CRI-O v1.20 or later The kubelet and the container runtime must both be configured to use the correct cgroup driver. See Configure the kubelet's cgroup driver to match the container runtime cgroup driver. For now, you can opt back in to use cgroup v1; the Kubernetes project recommends using cgroup v2, but in Kubernetes 1.36 (the current release) the cgroup v1 option remains supported as a fallback. That fallback is scheduled for removal in Kubernetes v1.38. If you are running an older cluster, plan to migrate; if you are setting up a new cluster with Linux nodes, you should prefer cgroup v2. In either case, review both the Kubernetes runtime documentation and (if relevant) the containerd compatibility matrix. kernel updates around cgroup v2When Kubernetes was first announced, in 2014, only v1 cgroup existed. Version 2 cgroup management first appeared in Linux kernel 4.5, released in 2016. In Linux 4.5, the cgroup v2 io, memory, and pids controllers were supported. Linux 4.15 added support for the cgroup v2 cpu controller. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) support began with Linux 4.20. The Kubernetes project does not recommend using cgroup v2 with a Linux kernel older than 5.2 due to lack of cgroup-level task freezer support. Kubernetes documents 5.8 as the minimum kernel version for cgroup v2; the root cgroup's system-level cpu.stat file was added in Linux 5.8. The memory.high livelock fix used by Memory QoS is present in Linux 5.9 and later. memory.peak was added in Linux 5.19. cgroup driver configurationConfigure the kubelet's cgroup driver to match the container runtime cgroup driver. If you use kubeadm to manage your cluster, Kubernetes recommends that you use the systemd cgroup driver, because kubeadm manages the kubelet as a systemd service. For other management tooling, check the documentation for the tool you're using to manage your cluster. If you can pick either option, I recommend using the systemd driver. Whatever tooling you've chosen, the kubelet automatically tries to detect the runtime's recommended cgroup driver. This automatic detection relies on using a runtime that implements the RuntimeConfig CRI RPC (for example: containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+). If you're using a container runtime that supports cgroup v2 but doesn't support automatic cgroup driver detection, you can manually configure an override by editing the kubelet configuration file. For example: apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: KubeletConfiguration cgroupDriver: systemd Automatic discovery of the runtime's cgroup driver through the CRI, tracked by KEP-4033, graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.34. It requires a runtime that implements the RuntimeConfig CRI RPC (containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+). When available, the kubelet uses the value reported by the runtime instead of its configured cgroupDriver value. Tools and commands for troubleshootingTools and commands that you should know about cgroups: stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup/: Check whether cgroup v2 is enabled; it returns cgroup2fs. systemctl list-units 'kube*' --type=slice or --type=scope: List Kubernetes-related units that systemd currently has in memory. bpftool cgroup list /sys/fs/cgroup/*: List all programs attached to the cgroup CGROUP. systemd-cgls /sys/fs/cgroup/*: Recursively show control group contents. systemd-cgtop: Show top control groups by their resource usage. tree -L 2 -d /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice: Show Pods' related cgroups directories. How to check if a Pod CPU or memory limit is successfully applied to the cgroup file?Work from the API object down to the node. Identify the node, then compare desired resources in the spec with the enacted values in status (in-place resize can leave those out of sync): kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}{"
"}' kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{range .spec.containers}{.name}{" spec	"}{.resources}{"
"}{end}' kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{range .status.containerStatuses}{.name}{" status	"}{.resources}{"
"}{end}' On that node, as root, with the systemd cgroup driver and cgroup v2 (these snippets also need jq). Pin the container with kubelet labels; a container name alone is not unique on a node. Use crictl ps -a if the container is not running: CONTAINER_ID=$(crictl ps \ --label io.kubernetes.pod.namespace=<namespace> \ --label io.kubernetes.pod.name=<pod-name> \ --name <container-name> -q | head -n1) # OCI view (not the CRI protobuf field names) crictl inspect "$CONTAINER_ID" | jq '.info.runtimeSpec.linux.resources' # Kernel cgroup path for this container PID=$(crictl inspect "$CONTAINER_ID" | jq -r '.info.pid') CGROUP="/sys/fs/cgroup$(awk -F: '$1=="0"{print $3}' /proc/$PID/cgroup)" cat "$CGROUP/cpu.weight" # request.cpu → shares → weight; not a limit cat "$CGROUP/cpu.max" # limit.cpu as "quota period"; unlimited is "max <period>" cat "$CGROUP/memory.max" # limit.memory; unlimited is "max" # Pod-level cgroup (parent slice), used by Pod-level resources cat "$(dirname "$CGROUP")/cpu.max" "$(dirname "$CGROUP")/memory.max" # Present when MemoryQoS is enabled cat "$CGROUP/memory.high" "$CGROUP/memory.min" "$CGROUP/memory.low" SCOPE=$(basename "$CGROUP") systemctl show "$SCOPE" \ -p CPUWeight -p CPUQuotaPerSecUSec -p CPUQuotaPeriodUSec -p MemoryMax Do not treat info.runtimeSpec.linux.cgroupsPath as a filesystem path when the runtime uses the systemd driver; that value is a systemd unit path (slice:runtime:id), not a directory under /sys/fs/cgroup. Expected mapping at each layer: Kubernetes: spec.containers.resources (desired) and status.containerStatuses.resources (enacted after in-place resize). Pod-level resources are on spec.resources and the parent pod slice. CRI (kubelet → runtime; these protobuf names stay cgroup v1-style even on v2): cpu_shares, cpu_quota, cpu_period, memory_limit_in_bytes, plus unified for Memory QoS. crictl inspect does not show these names; it shows the OCI spec the runtime derived from them. OCI spec: linux.resources.cpu.{shares,quota,period}, linux.resources.memory.limit, and linux.resources.unified. The runtime converts shares, quota, and period into cgroup v2 files. After upgrading crun or runc, the shares-to-weight formula may change; see CPU weight conversion. systemd scope: CPUWeight, CPUQuotaPerSecUSec, CPUQuotaPeriodUSec, MemoryMax. Unlimited or unset values often appear as  or infinity. cgroupfs: cpu.weight (from CPU request; an unset request still yields the default of 2 shares), cpu.max, and memory.max on the container scope. Memory QoS adds memory.high, memory.min, and memory.low. Further reading Kubernetes 1.31: Moving cgroup v1 Support into Maintenance Mode Kubernetes v1.36: Tiered Memory Protection with Memory QoS Kubernetes v1.36: PSI Metrics for Kubernetes Graduates to GA Kubernetes 1.25: cgroup v2 graduates to GA KubeCon NA 2022 cgroup v2: Before You Jump In by Tony Gosselin & Mike Tougeron, Adobe Systems KubeCon NA 2022 Cgroupv2 Is Coming Soon To a Cluster Near You - David Porter, Google & Mrunal Patel, RedHat KubeCon EU 2020 Kubernetes On cgroup v2 by Giuseppe Scrivano, Red Hat. This blog only covers the basic requirements and configuration of Kubernetes components. It will not include how to enable cgroup fs in OS distributions. For migration, you can refer to migrating cgroup v2

title: [Cloudflare] nginx2root: Five new nginx vulnerabilities, and how Cloudflare protects origins from the worst of them
summary: On November 18, 2026, F5 and nginx.org disclosed ten vulnerabilities in nginx. Five of them, detailed by the Xint research team and published under the name nginx2root, are memory corruption flaws that an unauthenticated attacker can use to crash an nginx worker or, per Xint's research, run commands on the server. Xint also found a Linux kernel bug that turns that foothold into root on the host, including from inside a Docker container. Other teams found the two HTTP/2 bugs independently: F5 also credits Rapid7, Wiz Research and Ikotas Labs for CVE-2026-123007, and Metnir, Wiz Research, and Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for CVE-2026-123633.nginx is an HTTP web server that also serves as reverse proxy, content cache, load balancer, TCP/UDP proxy server, and mail proxy server. nginx runs a large share of the world's web servers, so this is a patch-now event. But if your nginx server is reachable only through Cloudflare's proxy, attackers cannot reach the vulnerable code paths for the most serious of these bugs, giving you protection while you update your servers.Here is where Cloudflare stands, what that protection covers, where it stops, and how the bugs work.The short versionCloudflare's edge is not affected. Much of the proxy that handles customer traffic at our edge now runs on FL2, written in Rust. We reviewed the parts still built on our heavily modified nginx fork against all five bugs before disclosure, and an update closing the related code paths finished rolling out globally before the vulnerabilities were published. The same releases fix five other nginx CVEs, including CVE-2026-118899, an infinite loop while reading a request body over TLS 1.3.Origins behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy are shielded from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks. For proxied hostnames, Cloudflare terminates every client HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connection at our edge and opens a separate connection to your origin. The attacker's frames never reach your nginx.The resolver and mail proxy vulnerabilities depend on specific configuration. Many configurations of nginx will not be vulnerable, but the safest way to be sure is to update your install or disable features.You should still patch. Update to nginx 1.30.7 or 1.31.9 (or your vendor's fixed build) and restart. Some configurations, covered below, are not protected by the proxy.What was disclosednginx2root is five independent bugs. Each one works on its own and each one needs a different configuration.CVEBug classAffected configurationFirst affected releaseCVE-2026-123007Integer overflow leading to out-of-bounds heap read/writeHTTP/2 enabled1.9.5 (2015)CVE-2026-123633Use-after-freeHTTP/2 with proxy_pass to a backend, worker low on worker_connections1.19.7CVE-2026-121810Use-after-freeHTTP/3 (QUIC) with proxy_pass to a backend1.25.0CVE-2026-123634Use-after-freeresolver + proxy_pass with variables + a subrequest (mirror or SSI)0.6.18CVE-2026-113425Use-after-freeMail proxy with proxy on and auth_http0.5.33F5 rates each one High (CVSS 3.1: 8.1) and Critical (CVSS 4.0: 9.2), and notes that code execution requires disabling or bypassing ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization). For CVE-2026-123007, Xint's write-up shows how it leaked memory addresses to do exactly that.CVE-2026-123007 is the one to worry about most. It only needs HTTP/2 turned on, which is commonly enabled on TLS deployments, and it has been in every nginx release since HTTP/2 support shipped in 1.9.5. Xint ran the exploit over the public Internet against servers on AWS, GCP and Azure. Xint searched Shodan on November 10, before the disclosure, and found 56.7 million hosts matching product:nginx. Of the 11.94 million that reported a version, 98.9% fell in the affected range. As of November 19, Censys's nginx2root exposure tracker counts about 8.8 million services running a potentially affected version with HTTP/2 enabled. Version strings don't prove a host is vulnerable, since distributions backport fixes, but the exposure is large.The same nginx releases also fix five other bugs. The most serious, CVE-2026-118899, is an infinite loop when reading a request body over TLS 1.3 that lets an unauthenticated attacker stall a worker, in nginx 1.13.0 and later.The Linux kernel bug is the sixth part of nginx2root. Xint found a use-after-free in the kernel's SCTP send path, present since Linux 4.15 (2018): while a send operation waits, its SCTP association can be moved to another socket, and the waiting send can then free it. An attacker who already runs code as the nginx worker can use it to gain root on the host, and Xint did this from an nginx running inside a Docker container. Many distributions load the SCTP module automatically the first time a program opens an SCTP socket, so hosts that never use SCTP can still be exposed. As of November 18, no kernel fix was available and Xint was withholding the details until there is one.As of November 19, none of the five nginx2root CVEs is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and we have not seen reports of exploitation in the wild. Xint and Wiz Research have not released their exploits. Rapid7 has published a proof of concept, which it describes as suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started local container. Fake 'exploits' are also circulating on GitHub.Why Cloudflare's proxy protects your originnginx2root's most dangerous bugs live in how nginx parses and manages HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connections. To trigger them, an attacker has to send a carefully ordered stream of protocol frames directly to the nginx process: billions of WINDOW_UPDATE frames, a SETTINGS frame that holds response data back, PING frames that fill the send buffers, partial HEADERS frames, RST_STREAM at exactly the right moment.When your DNS record is proxied through Cloudflare, that connection ends at our edge.Cloudflare reads the client's HTTP request, applies your security and caching rules, and then makes its own request to your origin over a connection Cloudflare controls. The flow-control frames, pings, settings, and stream resets that the attacker sends are consumed by our edge. They are not forwarded. Your nginx only ever sees the requests Cloudflare chooses to send, framed the way Cloudflare frames them. This also holds when Cloudflare connects to your origin over HTTP/2: Cloudflare runs its own flow control on that connection and sends WINDOW_UPDATE and RST_STREAM frames only as its own traffic needs, so a client can't make it relay the billions of WINDOW_UPDATE frames the attack requires.Rapid7 makes the same point in its analysis of CVE-2026-123007: if the HTTP/2 connection is proxied, the attacker's frames "will likely not be retransmitted" in a way that allows exploitation. This breaks each of the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks.CVEWhat the attacker needsBehind Cloudflare's HTTP proxyCVE-2026-123007Direct control over HTTP/2 WINDOW_UPDATE, SETTINGS, PING and RST_STREAM on one connection to nginxProtected. Control frames terminate at Cloudflare's edge.CVE-2026-123633The first part of a HEADERS frame on a direct HTTP/2 connection, plus the ability to exhaust nginx connection slots and reset the TCP connectionProtected. The client's HTTP/2 connection terminates at Cloudflare.CVE-2026-121810A direct QUIC/HTTP/3 connection to nginxProtected. HTTP/3 terminates at Cloudflare's edge. We do not communicate to origins over HTTP/3CVE-2026-123634A request and its mirror or SSI subrequest waiting on the same DNS lookup, and the main request ending while the answer is processed. In Xint's exploit, nginx's resolver had to reach the attacker's DNS server.Not fully protected. Depends on how your config builds proxy_pass. Patch.CVE-2026-113425A direct IMAP/POP3/SMTP connection to the nginx mail proxyNot protected. Cloudflare's HTTP proxy does not carry mail traffic.There is one condition to be protected by Cloudflare here: your origin must not be reachable directly. If an attacker can find your origin's IP and connect to it directly (TCP 443 or 80 for HTTP/2, UDP 443 for HTTP/3, or the mail ports), Cloudflare isn't in the path and the protection doesn't apply. You should ensure that your origin servers can only be accessed through Cloudflare’s proxies, using one of the following approaches:Cloudflare Tunnel. Your origin makes an outbound-only connection to Cloudflare and exposes no inbound ports.Firewall to Cloudflare IP ranges. Accept inbound HTTP/HTTPS only from Cloudflare's published IP ranges. This must be done using an IP firewall, not based on configuration in your nginx server.Authenticated Origin Pulls (mTLS). Your origin rejects any TLS connection that doesn't present Cloudflare's client certificate.Xint's own exposure check makes the same point: "If a CDN or reverse proxy sits in front of nginx, the test only reaches the proxy, so also run it directly against the nginx server."Where the protection does not applyThere are several situations in which Cloudflare’s HTTP proxy does not provide protection.Spectrum TCP/UDP applications. For these configurations, traffic from the Internet is passed unmodified through to your origin. If your origin is running nginx, patch or disable the affected features.nginx mail proxy. Cloudflare's HTTP proxy does not carry IMAP, POP3 or SMTP. Restrict mail listeners to trusted networks until patched.CVE-2026-123634 (resolver). This depends on how your configuration builds the proxy_pass target from the request, combined with a carefully timed cancellation of an HTTP request. Passing your traffic through Cloudflare’s proxy makes it harder to exploit this, but does not provide full protection. Update regardless.DNS-only (grey-cloud), internal or non-proxied nginx. Any nginx server an attacker can reach without going through Cloudflare, including internal services behind a compromised host, needs to be patched.Cloudflare’s WAF rules are not relevant to these vulnerabilities. These are protocol-level bugs. Because Cloudflare’s proxy handles parsing the HTTP protocol messages, and creates new messages to fetch information from origin servers, origins behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy are protected from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 bugs without needing a rule. We have therefore not released a managed rule. The protection comes from connection termination, not from pattern matching.What to do nowFind every nginx server. Include nginx Plus, distribution packages, container images and appliances. Run nginx -V and nginx -T on each and note HTTP/2, HTTP/3/QUIC listeners, proxy_pass with variables plus SSI or mirror, and any mail block.Patch. Update nginx Open Source to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, nginx Plus to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1, or your distribution's fixed package. F5 lists nginx Plus R34 to R36 as affected with no fixed build, so move those to a fixed 37.x release. Then restart nginx or complete a binary upgrade. A config reload does not replace the running binary.Check backport versions carefully. Distributions often patch without changing the version nginx -v reports. Compare the full package version against your distribution's advisory.Make sure your origin is only reachable through Cloudflare. Use Tunnel, IP allowlisting or Authenticated Origin Pulls.If you can't patch yet, disable what you don't need. http2 off; (nginx 1.25.1 and later; on older versions, remove http2 from the listen directive) blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. Removing QUIC listeners and setting http3 off; blocks CVE-2026-121810. Point proxy_pass at fixed upstream groups for CVE-2026-123634. Don't rely on mirror_request_body alone: Xint's tested setup set it to off, and the default on stopped that exploit, but SSI and other subrequests can still reach the bug. Bind mail listeners to trusted networks for CVE-2026-113425. Restart so old connections close.Block SCTP if you don't use it. Add install sctp /bin/false to a file in /etc/modprobe.d/ to stop the kernel module from loading. This doesn't unload an already-loaded module or disable SCTP built into the kernel. When your distribution ships a kernel update for the SCTP bug, install it and reboot. Blocking the module is a stopgap until then.The Cloudflare Radar Zero Wire entry for nginx2root has the full checklist, a prompt you can give an agent to run a read-only assessment of your fleet, and links to every vendor advisory.Technical deep diveLet’s dig into the details of the five bugs by looking through the code. We’re looking at nginx 1.31.8 (commit 140aa94) which was the most recent code published before the fixes, and comparing this to the fixes in 1.31.9 (which were also included in release 1.30.7 on the stable branch).A note on methodology: we based our analysis on the public advisories, and to verify our reading of the code, we built the public 1.31.8 and 1.31.9 releases with AddressSanitizer and ran tests for four of the five bugs (flow control, HTTP/2 use-after-free, resolver and mail proxy). Each one faults on 1.31.8 and runs clean on 1.31.9. We did not reproduce the HTTP/3 bug; that section is based on the fix commit and the published analysis.One pattern, in four placesFour of the five bugs are use-after-free bugs. This is a common issue with programs that manually manage memory without language support: one part of the code frees an object that another part is still using.nginx is event driven. A handler runs, calls other code, and that code returns to the handler. Three of the bugs occur when the called code tears down the connection or request the handler is working on. In the fourth, a second connection still holds a pointer to the object.CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-121810. A request needs a connection slot to reach its upstream. nginx is low on slots, so it closes an idle connection to free one. The connection it chooses is the one the request belongs to.CVE-2026-123634. A resolver callback ends a request. Cleanup of that request frees a second resolver context that the resolver is about to call next.CVE-2026-113425. When a write to a mail client fails, the client connection is closed while the connection to the authentication service still points at its session.F5 rates all four as potential code execution if address space layout randomization (ASLR) is disabled or bypassed, and in its tests Xint reports code execution with the privileges of the nginx worker.The fifth bug, CVE-2026-123007, is of a different kind: an accounting error that becomes a length error. CVE-2026-123007: two flow-control pieces that each look correctHTTP/2 flow control limits the amount of response data a server may send. nginx tracks a send window for each stream and one for the connection, h2c->send_window. The client enlarges a window with a WINDOW_UPDATE frame, and the protocol caps every window at 2^31 − 1.nginx enforces that cap when a WINDOW_UPDATE arrives (ngx_http_v2_state_window_update()):if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window) { /* logs "client violated connection flow control" */ return ngx_http_v2_connection_error(h2c, NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR); }On its own, this check is correct. But the connection window also grows in a second place. When nginx queues DATA frames for a stream, it subtracts their length from the window. If the stream is canceled before those frames go out, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() takes them off the queue and returns the credit:h2c->send_window += window;Nothing caps this line. As the fix commit describes, if the client enlarges the connection window after the frames are queued and before the stream is terminated, the refund pushes the window past 2^31 − 1.From that point the first check no longer works. h2c->send_window is an unsigned size_t, so NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window wraps around to a very large number and every subsequent WINDOW_UPDATE is accepted. The client can then raise the window as far as it wants.The window is unsigned, but the code that sizes DATA frames compares it as a signed value (ngx_http_v2_send_chain()):if (limit == 0 || limit > (off_t) h2c->send_window) { limit = h2c->send_window; } ... if ((off_t) frame_size > limit) { frame_size = (size_t) limit; }After the window passes 2^63, it is negative as an off_t. The frame size becomes the window value itself, a number between 2^63 and 2^64, and nginx builds a buffer whose last pointer lies before its pos pointer.Over TLS, that buffer reaches a memcpy() in ngx_ssl_send_chain() with that length. Our TLS test stops at that point under AddressSanitizer. Xint's write-up explains how, with the window pushed close to 2^64, this turns into a controlled out-of-bounds write and an address leak, and Xint, Rapid7, and Wiz each report code execution from it. This post goes no further than the fault.Over cleartext HTTP/2, the same invalid buffer follows a different output path. Our cleartext test also faults under AddressSanitizer on 1.31.8 and runs clean on 1.31.9. The public write-ups address the TLS case.How much traffic the known attacks requireThe biggest step a WINDOW_UPDATE can take is 2^31 − 1, and a WINDOW_UPDATE frame is 13 bytes. Bringing a 64-bit window near its top therefore requires about 2^33 frames: roughly 8.6 billion frames, or about 112 GB (104 GiB).Rapid7, which published a proof of concept, gives the same figure and adds that nginx limits control-frame traffic relative to other traffic on the connection, so its run also sends about 15 GiB of other request traffic. Its total comes to approximately 128 GB of HTTP/2 data: about two minutes on a 10 Gbit/s link and about seventeen minutes at 1 Gbit/s. Rapid7 estimates the WINDOW_UPDATE traffic needed to reach 2^63 at about 2^32 frames, or 52 GiB, half of the 104 GiB figure. It also notes that these figures describe its route and are not a proven minimum.For defenders, this is the useful fact about the bug. At this volume, the known attacks are hard to hide: nginx receives tens of gigabytes from a single client over one long-lived connection and sends little back, much more than the requests in the access log account for.Why it was difficult to findThe refund line has existed in nginx since HTTP/2 support arrived in 1.9.5 in 2015.
