title: [Netflix] Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System
summary: By Shreya S Ramanujam, Yongce Li, Afshine Amidi, Sina Ghiassian, Benjamin Klein.IntroductionPicture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton. You log on to Netflix, search for “Bridgerton” and land on this screen:If this sounds familiar, you already know what a synopsis is — it’s a short glimpse into what a viewer can expect to see in a show. We see two types of synopses here: a series-level synopsis describing the overarching plot, and multiple episode-level synopses describing each episode.A synopsis plays a very important role for us — it helps viewers decide whether a title is worth watching or not. Every synopsis needs to strike a balance: sharing just enough to give viewers a sense of what to expect, while leaving enough intrigue to draw them in. But of course, we can’t just write anything.“In the fog-drenched streets of Victorian London, Detective Daphne Bridgerton races to unmask a serial killer known only as the elusive Lady Whistledown.”Intriguing? Definitely. But it is most certainly not the premise of Bridgerton. Which leads us to the first (and most important) rule of writing a good synopsis: it must be factual. At Netflix’s scale, with thousands of titles, multiple episodes per season and multiple languages, fact-checking all of these by hand simply doesn’t scale. This is where our factuality service comes in: an automated way to judge whether a synopsis is factual or not.Our current factuality checker feeds a reasoning model everything we know about a title (like metadata and text assets) and asks it to judge synopsis factuality according to a rigorous rubric. There are two main limitations of this approach that we want to optimize:High cost of long-context reasoning calls: Each decision requires expensive, long-context model calls to reasoning models, which doesn’t scale well when we want to check multiple titles, episodes, languages, and style variants.Misaligned rationales: The model’s explanations often diverge from our annotators’ reasoning, which makes its factuality verdicts less reliable. We want these rationales to be better aligned so that (1) the model can consistently flag nuanced errors, and (2) its explanations can be used downstream to automatically correct issues in the synopsis.Our new approach tackles both problems at once. On the cost side, it delivers a 52.4% reduction per synopsis. On the quality side, it significantly improves both verdict accuracy and reasoning alignment: Recall–Fail (“Of all truly non-factual synopses, how many does the system correctly reject?”) rises from 0.77 to 0.86, and the new factuality service’s explanations now show ~82% overlap with human rationales (up from ~69%). In other words, it’s not just cheaper and more accurate — it’s also much better aligned with how our expert annotators actually judge synopses.So, what exactly does factuality mean?Let’s go back to the Bridgerton example. Say you see this synopsis about Bridgerton Season 1:Synopsis A: “Bridgerton follows Daphne Bridgerton, the eldest daughter of the powerful Bridgerton family as she makes her debut onto Regency London’s competitive marriage market.”It’s easy to judge that this synopsis is factually correct — no wrong facts, and it gives the reader a clear, accurate glimpse of what to expect from the show.Let’s take another example:Synopsis B: “Set in modern-day London, this gritty crime drama follows Detective Daphne Bridgerton as she hunts a serial killer while hiding her own criminal past.”Another easy one — the plot is so blatantly off the mark that it is definitely not factual.But what about this?Synopsis C: “Bridgerton follows the mysterious, sharp-tongued Lady Whistledown as she exposes the secrets of London’s high society through her scandalous gossip sheet.”Technically, every statement here is true — Lady Whistledown does indeed publish a gossip sheet, and if there’s one thing she is known for, it’s her scathing exposés. So then, is this a factual synopsis?Not quite! While technically true, it paints a misleading picture of the show. A new viewer might reasonably expect it to revolve around Lady Whistledown, rather than Daphne navigating the marriage market. This, too, is a type of non-factuality we want to catch.Lastly, here’s the trickiest of all:Synopsis D: “When Daphne Bridgerton makes her society debut, she catches the eye of the aloof Duke of Hastings, and the two begin a passionate love affair that sets the whole ton abuzz.”Again, every statement is true, but the phrasing is misleading. A new viewer might assume they fall in love immediately, missing the fact that their relationship begins as a fake, mutually beneficial arrangement. This is another type of nuanced error our system should flag.So now that we have an idea of the kinds of errors we care about, the real question is: how do we build a system that is able to catch both glaring as well as subtle factuality violations?Current Service and Its LimitationsOur current factuality pipeline is a straightforward, holistic LLM call. We feed a reasoning model everything we know about a title (text assets, metadata, and a detailed factuality rubric) and ask it to judge the factuality of a synopsis. We repeat the call several times to reduce output randomness, and if any run flags the synopsis as non-factual, it fails. This approach has two main limitations:High cost: Each judgment requires multiple (five, to be exact) calls to a large reasoning model over extremely long contexts (100k+ tokens), which does not scale well.Misaligned reasoning: The model can fail synopses for nitpicky reasons (e.g., “This is a show about wonderful magic” gets failed because the characters never literally call the magic “wonderful”) while overlooking nuanced errors by convincing itself they “don’t really make the synopsis false.” This misalignment makes verdicts less reliable and rationales less useful for downstream correction.Optimizing the Holistic PipelineTo understand exactly where we should optimize the current holistic pipeline, we study the current pipeline both qualitatively and quantitatively on a custom factuality benchmark that we built. This benchmark comprises synopses hand-labeled by human annotators as factual or non-factual, along with their rationales. This analysis reveals several key insights:Insight 1: Do we really need five holistic calls?Let’s think back to why we added multiple holistic calls in the first place: to reduce sampling noise. In practice, though, we see an interesting dichotomy:Blatantly true / false synopses (Bridgerton A, B): All runs agree on the verdict with near-identical reasoning.Nuanced errors (Bridgerton C, D): The model is much more likely to disagree with itself — some runs catch the error, some don’t. This is exactly where additional sampling helps.This suggests a simple optimization: A and B don’t really need all 5 calls. If we can somehow identify these “easy” synopses upfront, we can cut down on the number of calls for them, while still giving harder cases like C and D the extra calls they need.The easiest way to do this is to ask the model to output its confidence alongside its verdict and rationale. We can then separate “easy” (high confidence) synopses from “hard” (low confidence) ones and only send the hard cases through additional checks. Think of it like airport security: most bags go straight through, but those that trigger the alarm (low confidence) get extra screening.Implementing this easy fix makes our pipeline go from the current holistic model to a new “confidence gated” holistic model:Insight 2: Five identical judges calls give us no new informationWith confidence gating, our pipeline only escalates harder synopses to the full five holistic calls. But extra calls only help with sampling noise, not systematic reasoning errors: if every run follows the same flawed rationale, they’ll all reach the same wrong verdict, rendering the extra calls useless. How can we ensure that each call counts?Idea: Diversify the judges and make them specializedInstead of running five holistic judges with the same generic factuality prompt, we introduce two specialized judges that individually target the two aspects of factuality we care about:Literal Judge: Is the synopsis literally true?Implicature Judge: Does this synopsis give a false picture to a new reader who has not watched this show?Explicitly searching for specific types of errors helps us better flag both literal and subtler implicature errors. In practice, we observe that this works better than repeatedly querying a single holistic judge, hoping that sampling stochasticity will surface nuanced errors.Insight 3: The rationale reveals mistakes the verdict hidAt this point, we have a pretty good pipeline, but we’re still underusing one of the richest signals available to us: the model’s rationale behind its verdict. For nuanced errors, we often see the model identify a point of contention, then brush it aside based on a faulty assumption or because it deems the issue too minor to affect the verdict. Can we use these shaky spots in the rationale to catch (and correct) errors the verdict misses?Idea: Secondary atomic-claim checking via a router:Since our literal and implicature judges are already strong reasoning models, we ask them to additionally critically analyse their own reasoning and surface shaky spots — any doubts, concessions, or assumptions that might need rechecking. These include cases where the model:Makes an assumption.Raises a doubt that the available evidence can’t resolve (e.g., an external critic quote).Notices a contradiction but dismisses it as insufficient to change the verdict.We pass all concessions from both judges to a router model, which:Reframes them as self-contained, verifiable atomic claims, each with a materiality field specifying the evidence needed to support or refute it.Routes each claim to the appropriate secondary Stage-2 judge: a web judge for external facts (e.g., citations, media quotes, or prior work), or a source-material recheck focused on the reframed atomic claim. By pinpointing the exact point of contention, the recheck is more targeted, making it easier to mark the claim as true or false.Putting It All Together: Proposed Cascade Factuality ServiceOur findings lead to three key improvements: specialized judges, confidence-gated escalation, and targeted rechecking of shaky reasoning using a secondary stage when escalated.We implement these improvements as a tiered system shown in the figure below: every synopsis first passes through both the literal and the implicature judges. High-confidence verdicts are retained, while low-confidence cases escalate to the router and Stage-2 judges for further checking. Stage 2 can overturn the initial verdict in two cases:FAIL → PASS: All concessions, including the original failure reasons, are supported by the secondary check.PASS → FAIL: At least one concession is contradicted.ResultsBased on our discussions from above, we evaluate three different pipelines:Evaluation: Datasets and MetricsWe evaluate these systems on two datasets: show-level and episode-level synopses. Each datapoint includes a synopsis, a human gold label (factual / not factual), and the annotator’s rationale. For episode-level synopses, we additionally require that the synopsis be specific to that particular episode, not just a generic synopsis of the overall show.We focus on two main axes: Quality and Cost. The quality metrics are listed below:Recall-FAIL is our primary metric: higher recall means fewer Gold FAILs are missed. We also track Precision-PASS, which measures how reliably PASS verdicts identify Gold PASSes, and alignment with human rationales.On the cost side, we want to reduce both the average number of LLM calls per synopsis and the end-to-end cost of producing a final verdict. Latency is not our primary optimization target, but we do want to ensure the median (P50) latency does not blow up to impractical judgement times.Evaluation ResultsThe best numbers per metric per dataset are shown in bold.Note: We compared the cascade against two holistic ablations — increased reasoning effort and a smaller, cheaper model — to test if simple ablations could achieve better performance. For episode-level synopses, we also added a full-show summary to the prompt to provide context from previous episodes; we observe summaries substantially improve performance when compared to non-summary context variants, so we report only summary-based variants.Our takeaways from this experiment are:Cascade improves quality. Our primary metric, Recall-FAIL improves on both show and episode level synopses, with a limited impact on Recall-PASS. In other words, we now catch more Gold FAIL synopses without sacrificing the reliability of our PASS verdicts.Cascade is cheaper. Cascade cuts total cost by 52.4% on the show-level dataset. Cascade (with summary) is also 15% cheaper than the current (no summary) holistic pipeline on episodic dataset.Cascade’s P50 latency increases with respect to the holistic baseline. Even so, this remains within what we consider a reasonable range for factuality judgment.Simple tweaks aren’t enough. Increasing reasoning effort makes the factuality checker too lenient, while using a smaller model makes it too strict — neither addresses the underlying problems of the holistic baseline.Summary context matters for episodic tasks. Without a full-show summary, the model tends to over-fail because it lacks the context to determine whether a detail from the episode summary fits the broader storyline.Alignment with Human RationaleSo far, we’ve established that the cascade produces better verdicts: it catches more non-factual synopses and produces more reliable PASS decisions. But are these verdicts correct for the right reasons?To measure this, we use an LLM-as-a-Judge to compare each pipeline’s reasoning against the human rationale on Gold-FAIL (GF) synopses. The judge assigns a Reasoning Similarity Score (RSS) of 0 (dissimilar), 0.5 (partially similar), or 1 (very similar) based on rationale overlap.We observe that cascade is significantly better aligned with human rationale in all cases. This is a big gain — not only is the cascade giving us more accurate factuality verdicts, but it also identifies the same points of contention in the synopsis as a specialized human annotator.Conclusion + Future WorkOverall, our proposed cascade pipeline improves both cost and quality of the existing factuality service:On the cost side, confidence gating lets us avoid unnecessary calls, reducing the average cost of factuality evaluation.On the quality side, two diverse judges allow us to collect complementary informative verdicts, while the Stage-2 judges recheck and correct the assumptions behind uncertain decisions. This results in higher verdict accuracy and substantially better alignment between model and expert annotator reasoning.The cascade gives us a path toward a factuality system that is not just more accurate, but also more interpretable and self-correcting. Some future directions to consider would be:Adding multimodal inputs to help verify claims that text assets alone cannot confirm.Use the rationale from factuality checking to correct the faulty synopsis.Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Netflix] Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing
summary: Serdar Cellat, Yuchen Xie, Bernadette Marcu, Blaid Burgess, Cody Jarrett, Carlos Pereira, Qing Shi, Samuel Carvajal, Manuel Pamplona, Dorothy Jung, Feiko Ritsema, Benjamin Klein, Alex Woo, Eugene Lok, Anna Pulido, Rebecka Swe, Sanford Holsapple, Ranjith Kumar ShettyIntroductionClips in the Netflix mobile app.At Netflix, a crucial part of our mission is ensuring our content looks stunning on any device. Vertical formats are increasingly important for Netflix, as we have 1.2B followers across our social media accounts, and have recently rolled out Clips, our vertical video feed in the Netflix mobile app. Traditionally, creating vertical assets meant editors and producers manually reframed horizontal videos in editing tools, a process that doesn’t scale as our catalog and use cases grow. To support both our in‑app feed and external marketing campaigns at scale, we built an automated multi‑ratio video cropping system, tightly integrated into our internal production tools, that can generate high‑quality vertical and other aspect‑ratio variants with minimal manual effort.Our Video Resizing ApproachConverting cinematic 16:9 footage into mobile‑friendly aspect ratios takes more than a simple center crop. Filmmaking often involves dynamic character blocking and complex camera movement. We need an intelligent “virtual camera” that can follow the key action, respond to how each scene is composed, and produce crops that feel as intentional as the original shot.We address this challenge by framing video resizing as a tracking and temporal optimization problem. Our pipeline processes each asset in three main stages, designed to produce 9:16, 4:5, and 1:1 crops in a single pass, without incurring additional computational overhead.An overview of the three-stage process converting horizontal footage into mobile aspect ratios.Shot Detection and SplittingFirst, we segment the video into atomic shots using a neural‑network–based shot boundary detector. In many cases, shots contain multiple characters conversing on opposite sides of the frame. To better handle these scenarios, we use an Active Speaker Detection based approach to logically split a single continuous shot into multiple sub‑shots. This allows our virtual camera to cut and re-focus on different speakers as the conversation flows. Our Active Speaker Detection leverages an internal face detector and LipFlap to reliably identify active speakers in both live‑action and animated titles.Shot splitting via Active Speaker Detection. The magenta box represents the dynamic vertical crop.Focus Region DiscoveryOnce shots and sub‑shots are defined, we identify the most important region in each frame. We combine face detections with visual saliency maps to filter and prioritize the faces that should be in focus. In scenes with multiple characters, we further rank faces using signals such as active speaker status and relative size. Our model aggregates these cues with shot‑level content understanding to establish a continuous “focus region” for the virtual camera.Blue box shows the focus region around the primary character for reframing.Temporal ReframingOnce we’ve established the focus region, the next challenge is deciding how the crop should move over time. Tracking the focus region on a strict frame-by-frame basis would produce a shaky, distracting viewing experience, so we apply a set of heuristics that consider how the focus region moves over the course of a shot. When its displacement is small, we lock a static crop window that consistently covers the relevant area. When there is significant motion, we compute a dynamic tracking window and smooth its path so that any panning feels intentional and cinematic.The vertical crop (magenta box) follows the character’s movement with a smooth panning path.Tooling and Workflow IntegrationWe integrated the resizing algorithm directly into our internal Clips tool, so editors and producers can access it as part of their existing workflow. The interface enables them to automatically generate multiple aspect‑ratio versions of a clip with smart reframing. A unified in‑app module provides intuitive shot‑reframing controls, allowing users to review the algorithm’s crops, and quickly make targeted adjustments where needed.For more complex shots or custom campaigns, producers can export the resizing parameters as XML and load them directly into external timeline editors such as Adobe Premiere. This allows agencies and external partners to start from the algorithm’s framing decisions instead of recreating crops manually or relying on tools like Premiere’s Auto Reframe. In our internal test, our resizing algorithm outperforms Auto Reframe on a curated evaluation set, so the XML export effectively brings those higher‑quality crops into external workflows. By bringing automated resizing and manual refinement into a single place, this pipeline significantly reduces production time and manual effort while preserving creative control.Video resizing interface with reframing controlsConclusionOur work on multi-ratio video resizing is one step in a broader effort to make content creation more scalable, without compromising creative intent. By pairing algorithm-driven reframing with editor-friendly tools, we’ve reduced the time teams spend on repetitive resizing tasks and unlocked faster experimentation across mobile feeds and marketing campaigns. As we continue to broaden these capabilities to new formats and workflows, our goal remains the same: to give creatives more time to tell great stories, and to deliver a consistently high-quality viewing experience for our members and fans.Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Netflix] Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes
summary: By Roberto Perez Alcolea, Java Platform TeamQuasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decisionAt Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed.The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it.Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next:Does any consumer still call this method?Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations?Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact?Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign?At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds.Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally.We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions:What changed in the library’s public API?Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed?The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing.From API Changes to Consumer ImpactExisting techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive.Quasar builds on SCIP, an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently.On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change.During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings through its REST and GraphQL APIs and MCP server; follow-up usage queries provide dependency-version breakdowns and source locations. A separate compatibility-impact assessment can also follow implementations and their callers when a producer supplies a changed JVM symbol.Consider this simplified API change:public interface Client {- Result getLegacyValue(Request request);+ Result getValue(Request request, Options options);}For a detailed compatibility-impact assessment of this removal, a producer-side tool supplies the old method descriptor. Quasar constructs its canonical symbol identity. This abridged excerpt from the direct-reference portion of Quasar’s Amazon Athena query shows the essential match:SELECT c.change_id, 'DIRECT_REFERENCE' AS evidence_kind, r.scm_type, r.org, r.repo, r.dep_version, r.file_pathFROM requested_changes cJOIN quasar.symbol_refs r ON r.symbol_canonical = c.target_canonicalrequested_changes contains the API changes submitted by the producer. The SQL excerpt finds repositories that call the removed method. Quasar also checks implementations and calls through them, so it can count each affected repository once. It returns sample dependency versions and file locations to help investigate the result.For the Client change, this tells the producer which repositories still use getLegacyValue, which versions they use, and where some of those calls occur. That helps the producer decide whether to coordinate a migration before removing the method.Bringing the Analysis Before ReleaseVersion-to-version comparison is valuable when planning an upgrade or writing a migration guide. Producers benefit even more when feedback arrives during code review.For pull-request analysis, Quasar stores API definition snapshots keyed by commit. Given a base and head commit, it classifies symbols as added, removed, or signature-modified. Removals and modifications then become candidates for consumer-impact analysis.An incompatible change is not automatically a high-risk change. Quasar reports the observed impact so the producer can decide what to do; it does not enforce a release policy. “No references observed” means only that Quasar found none in the indexed population. Reflection, configuration, dynamic loading, stale branches, or incomplete indexing can hide consumers. The result needs to show whether the requested commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated.Pull-request review requires indexed snapshots for the exact base and head commits. If either is unavailable, Quasar reports that it cannot compare them; it does not substitute a default-branch snapshot. This keeps a missing comparison from looking like a clean API diff.Return to our Client change. This illustrative report brings together signals available through Quasar's API comparison, consumer-usage queries, and library-level criticality. It is not a literal response from one API:{ "change": "REMOVED", "symbol": "Client#getLegacyValue(Request)", "affectedRepositories": 137, "versionDistribution": , "sampleConsumerLocations":  }, { "repository": "client-wrapper", "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/client/ClientAdapter.java", "lines":  } ], "libraryCriticality": { "tier": 1, "basis": "highest-tier downstream application" }, "comparison": { "baseShaFound": true, "headShaFound": true }}An impact report shows 137 affected repositories distributed across library versions 4.2.1, 4.1.7, and 3.9.4.The repository count is symbol-specific: in this example, 137 indexed repositories refer to the removed method. The version distribution reveals a dominant cohort on 4.2.1 and a smaller long tail still on 3.9.4. A producer can inspect affected repositories and retrieve indexed file paths, with line numbers where the index provides them. The JSON shows only two sample locations to keep the example readable. The filePath and lines shape mirrors Quasar's query contract. The tier is broader context about the library, inherited from its highest-criticality downstream application; it does not imply that all 137 callers are Tier 1.Together, those signals change the producer’s plan. Instead of merging the removal and waiting for failures, the producer can retain and deprecate the old method, publish a migration path, coordinate a broader migration, and track the long-tail versions before removal. File paths and available line numbers turn that scope into a concrete work list for engineers or coding agents. The same API diff paired with weak or stale evidence would lead to a different action: refresh the indexes before deciding. The value is not merely detecting the removal; it is choosing a proportionate next step.A pre-release workflow enriches API changes with consumer impact and evidence quality before the producer decides how to proceedA Polyglot Foundation with SCIPThe shared SCIP format also lets Quasar index several language ecosystems. Each language indexer resolves its own code, while Quasar can use the resulting symbol identities to find references across repositories.Conceptually, client-lib indexes Client#getLegacyValue(Request) as a definition, while checkout-service indexes a reference to the same symbol. Quasar can then connect the library API to its consumer across repositories.Language-specific indexers emit SCIP definitions, references, and relationships into Quasar’s shared semantic graph.Relationships are especially useful when generated code separates the API a producer owns from the symbols consumers invoke. For example, Quasar can trace a Protobuf definition through its generated Java members to the repositories that use them, even when consumer code never names the .proto element.SCIP records symbols and their references; it does not determine whether an API change violates an ecosystem’s compatibility rules. Today, Quasar compares indexed JVM and Protobuf API definitions and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java to find affected repositories. A separate JVM compatibility-impact path uses breaks identified by a producer-side tool to query affected repositories. Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust support usage queries, but Quasar does not yet assess their breaking API changes.Moving Risk Assessment EarlierToday, Quasar surfaces API-change findings on pull requests, including observed consumer counts and confidence. Producers can use its other queries to inspect dependency versions and source locations, with library criticality as broader context. Together, those signals support a decision before merge.We want to move that context earlier. An agent writing library code should recognize when it is changing a public symbol and consult Quasar before the change becomes a pull request. Quasar’s APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration provide an access path, but access alone does not create awareness. The coding workflow must also recognize public API edits so the agent knows when to query impact and when to involve the producer.Today Quasar assesses risk on a pull request. The future workflow gives agents consumer-impact context while they write code, before the pull request is opened.Earlier guidance will not replace pull-request analysis. The PR assessment will still verify the concrete diff and catch changes that were not recognized during coding. Coverage, freshness, ambiguity, unsupported platforms, and truncation must travel through both checks in machine-readable form. An agent should not turn “no observed usages in the available index” into “safe to remove.”Today, agents can query Quasar through MCP when prompted. We are working toward making that context part of the coding workflow, then using identified call sites to prepare migration changes. Quasar supplies semantic evidence, an agent reduces migration toil, and the library producer remains responsible for API and release decisions.What We LearnedBuilding this workflow led us to four practical lessons.Separate compatibility from reach. A removed method can break the API contract even when Quasar finds no callers. A list of affected repositories and their library versions shows the migration work ahead. Producers need both signals to choose a release path.Make the evidence inspectable. A repository count is more useful with sample call sites and a version breakdown. The result also needs to show which commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated. Otherwise, “no usage found” can be mistaken for proof that nobody is affected.Keep usage and compatibility separate across languages. SCIP lets Quasar find symbol references in several ecosystems. Deciding whether an API change is breaking requires compatibility rules or a trusted producer-side signal for that ecosystem.Bring evidence to the producer while choices are open. Pull-request findings can prompt a producer to retain an API, publish a migration path, or coordinate consumers before merge. Moving the same evidence into the coding workflow could shape the edit earlier. After release, it still helps locate consumers that need to migrate.Today, Quasar indexes JVM, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust code for cross-repository usage analysis. It compares JVM APIs and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java. Producers can review change findings through Quasar’s REST and GraphQL APIs or its MCP server, then investigate affected repositories and call sites. We are extending this foundation toward more ecosystem-specific compatibility checks, deeper code-review integration, and agent-assisted consumer migrations that keep release approval with the producer.Quasar is internal to Netflix, but the pattern is portable: index code semantically, retain API definitions, compare them at the point of change, query affected consumers, and report the quality of the evidence. Library producers need more than a compatibility verdict. They need to know who may be affected and have enough time to act before release.A huge thank you to the Java Platform team at Netflix. Their expertise, collaboration, and support made this work possibleRelated TalksFrom Lag to Lightning: Transforming Dependency Update Timelines explores how Netflix shortened dependency-update timelines.Netflix’s Journey to Confident Automated Code Changes discusses building confidence in automated changes at scale.Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Docker] Docker patches Java4Shell and the NGINX HTTP/2 with Docker Hardened Images
summary: OpenJDK and Oracle disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) on November 17, and NGINX released fixes for two HTTP/2 flaws the next day. Docker began publishing fixed images for both in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog starting that same day. What we know about Java4Shell is that it’s a memory-corruption bug in the Java runtime that can let an attacker with no credentials run code inside a Java application. Many container images contain a Java runtime, including application images that bundle their own, so it affects teams well beyond the ones that write Java. Docker Hardened Images are the trusted foundation your applications should run on, because a flaw in the runtime inside an image is fixed only when that image is rebuilt, and Docker rebuilds its hardened images as soon as upstream fixes become available. Fixed images for the Amazon Corretto, SapMachine and Azul Zulu runtimes and for NGINX are in the catalog today, with Eclipse Temurin following as soon as Adoptium completes its fixed builds. TL;DR Affected: Java 17.0.6 and later, including Java 21, 25, 26 and 27, from every OpenJDK vendor. Only on some hardware: the bug is reachable only when the JVM runs on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI. The same image can be exposed on one host and not on another. Fixes are arriving vendor by vendor. Corretto, SapMachine and Zulu builds in DHI are fixed. Temurin, which many DHI application images use, is not released yet. Check the version the runtime reports. A tag or a recent rebuild date does not tell you which Java build is inside an image. java -version does. Until your image runs a fixed build, start Java with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. Set it yourself and check that it took effect. Make sure it reaches every JVM, not only the first one. The second half of this post shows how. The NGINX HTTP/2 flaws are fixed in the catalog. The Docker Hardened Images for NGINX are rebuilt on NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. Pull the image again, or move a pinned tag to one of those versions, and redeploy. What the vulnerability is To decode Base64 quickly, the HotSpot JVM uses a hand-written routine built on AVX-512 instructions. That routine miscalculates a length when the input ends in unexpected padding and writes up to 62 bytes past the end of a buffer on the Java heap. Calif, the researchers who found it, turned that into heap disclosure and remote code execution. They demonstrated code execution before authentication against default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and after authentication against Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. They note there is no universal exploit: each application needs its own, and they have not published those. As of November 18 there are no public reports of exploitation in the wild. Oracle rates the issue 8.1 (High) under CVSS 3.1. The researchers rate it 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0. CISA has issued an alert urging immediate patching. How to find out if you’re exposed Java version. The JVM is 17.0.6 or later and does not yet include the fix. The fixed OpenJDK versions are 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1. Vendors add their own suffixes, but in the builds we checked, the build string printed by java -version contains one of those four numbers when the runtime is fixed. CPU. The host is x86-64 and supports AVX-512 VBMI: Intel Xeon from Ice Lake onward, AMD EPYC and Ryzen from Zen 4 onward. ARM64 hosts are not affected. Reachability. Data an attacker controls reaches Java’s Base64 decoder. That includes Authorization headers, tokens, SAML messages and file uploads. A Java client that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server is also in scope. For anything that accepts network input, assume this is true. All three of these must be true To check a host’s CPU, run this on the host or Kubernetes node. Hardened runtime images have no shell, so it will not run inside the container. grep -m1 ‘^flags’ /proc/cpuinfo | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep -E ‘^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$’ The host is affected if all four flags are printed. Two other ways to check, for when a shell on the node is hard to get. Ask the JVM. The fixed build can only come from whoever builds your image, because the Java runtime and the system packages your application runs on come from the image underneath it. That dependency is why a hardened image is a necessary step toward a trusted software supply chain. For most deployments, set JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS on the container:docker run -e JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=”-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics” <your-image>env: – name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS value: “-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics”Three cases need more care, and the next section covers them: images that already set Java option variables (our FIPS images do), environments that also run Java 8, and anything that starts more than one JVM.Prefer this flag to -XX:UseAVX=2, the other published mitigation. The researchers note that a proxy which buffers whole request bodies gets in the way of some of their exploits but not all of them, so do not count on it. Watch for crashes, and think about secrets. A failed attempt can crash the JVM. In the container log a crash starts like this:# A fatal error has been detected by the Java Runtime Environment:## SIGSEGV (0xb) at pc=0x…, pid=1, tid=…The JVM also writes a report named hs_err_pid<pid>.log inside the container. Making the flag reach every JVM A container often runs more than one JVM, for example when a build tool forks a JVM for tests, an application server starts helper processes or a CI agent starts a JVM for every build step. Watch out for JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS The JVM itself, however it is started. Includes javac, keytool and other JDK tools. Yes, through the inherited environment A Java 8 JVM that sees it refuses to start. Some DHI FIPS images already set this variable. JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS Only the java launcher, Java 9 and later Yes, when the child is started with java Not read by javac, keytool or other JDK tools. DHI FIPS images set it. Java 8 ignores it. The java command line That one JVM No Nothing downstream inherits it. JAVA_OPTS, JENKINS_JAVA_OPTS, MAVEN_OPTS, ES_JAVA_OPTS and similar A start script, which copies the value onto one java command line No Each script has its own rules. If nothing in the image reads the variable, it does nothing. Five rules follow from that table. We tested each on DHI images. JAVA_OPTS only works where a script reads it. With JAVA_OPTS=”-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics” set and a plain java command, the intrinsic stays on. No warning is printed. A flag on the command line stops at that process. We started a JVM with the flag on its command line and had it start a second JVM. The child ran with the intrinsic on. With JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS in the environment, the child ran with it off. A child started with a cleared environment gets nothing, whichever variable you use. Check what the image already sets before you set anything. In Docker and Kubernetes, your value replaces the image’s value. It is not appended. docker inspect –format ‘{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}’ <image> \ | grep -E ‘^(JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS|JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS)=’ Our FIPS images use these variables to configure the FIPS provider. dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:21-fips sets both. When we replaced its JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS with only the flag, the JVM started normally, but the org.bouncycastle.fips.approved_only property was gone. Nothing warned us. Keep JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS away from Java 8. Java 8 is not affected and does not know the flag: Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -XX:-UseBASE64IntrinsicsUnrecognized VM option ‘UseBASE64Intrinsics’Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine. Java 11 accepts the flag, so it is harmless there. Verify the process, not the environment. Running java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version inside a container starts a new JVM. It tells you what the environment gives a new JVM, not what the JVM already serving traffic was started with. For the running process, use the startup log line. JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS prints one too, starting with NOTE: Picked up. In an image that includes the JDK you can also ask the process directly: jcmd <pid> VM.flags | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics The answer must be -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. If the flag reached the JVM through an environment variable, it will not show in the process’s command line, so ps is not a reliable check. Some applications discard these variables on purpose. Elasticsearch’s start script, for example, ignores JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and expects ES_JAVA_OPTS. Check your application’s documentation. When the fixed images arrive Pull the new image and redeploy. Four things catch people out: The tag may not change. dhi.io/amazoncorretto:21.0.13 now reports the fixed Corretto-21.0.13.1.2, a newer build than the tag name suggests. A tag cannot tell you which build you are running. java -version can. Kubernetes may not pull. With imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent, the default for every tag except latest, a node that already holds the old image under that tag keeps using it, even after a restart. Deploy by digest, or set the policy to Always for this rollout. Mirrors lag. If you copy DHI into your own registry, the fix arrives when your mirror next syncs. Your own images need a rebuild. An image built FROM a DHI Java image keeps the old runtime until you rebuild and redeploy it. Then confirm with java -version that what is running reports a fixed build. After that, remove the flag from every place you set it. The NGINX HTTP/2 flaws are fixed in the same catalog The day after Java4Shell, NGINX released fixes for two memory errors in the way it handles HTTP/2 connections, tracked as CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. A crafted request can crash a worker process, and where an attacker gets past the operating system’s memory protections it can run code inside that worker. Both flaws need HTTP/2 to be enabled on the server, and the same releases fix other NGINX issues that do not depend on HTTP/2, so update either way. The Docker Hardened Images for NGINX were rebuilt on NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 and published on November 18, the same day as the upstream release. To patch, pull the image again and redeploy, and move any tag pinned to an older exact version to a fixed one. nginx -v prints the version, and the fixed ones are 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. The notes on pull policy, mirrors and your own images in the section above apply to NGINX images in the same way. Whether that code can be reached in your deployment depends on things an image cannot see: the CPU it is scheduled onto, the options you start it with, the processes it starts, and the traffic you send it. Pull the fixed images, redeploy, and confirm the Java version that is actually running. Make sure the flag is set on every JVM that is still waiting for a fixed runtime. Know which CPUs your workloads run on, control what can reach your Java services, and patch the JVMs you add yourself. So how many more bullets are you willing to dodge? It was only four weeks ago that the news was PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Calif, the security research team that found Java4Shell and helped find PHP2Shell, says it used AI to find this flaw in about an hour and that the whole effort cost less than $200 in tokens. When a flaw like this can be found and weaponized at that price, it is reasonable to expect more of them. If you lead a team or answer for how your organization builds and ships software, the questions after a week like this one are whether you were exposed and how quickly you can prove you were not. It is imperative to have a trusted foundation in place before the next flaw appears, and Docker Hardened Images is that foundation to adopt. This week Docker began publishing fixed Java and NGINX images to the catalog within a day of each disclosure, with the images still waiting listed in the status table above. Each image ships with a signed SBOM and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, so you have a record of what it contains and how it was built. The Docker Hardened Images catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, and moving one of your services onto a hardened image typically means changing one line in its Dockerfile. If you are not building on Docker Hardened Images yet, start today.

title: [GitLab] Keep recurring work moving with scheduled automations
summary: Every engineering team has work that needs regular attention, like triaging new issues or investigating incidents. Among DevSecOps professionals using AI tools, 43% say automating repetitive tasks has created the most efficiency, according to GitLab’s Global DevSecOps report. But agents still rely on a human to kick off the workflow or an event trigger to fire, and without a record of what ran and why, no one can trace how the work got done.With scheduled automations, in beta in GitLab 19.6, flows in GitLab Duo Agent Platform handle routine tasks on a schedule your team sets and keep a history of what ran. Scheduled automations are a building block of the governed software factory, where agents and flows work autonomously within controls set by your team.Put routine work on a scheduleRelying on a person or an event to start automated work limits efficiency gains and makes timing unpredictable. When the person responsible is out, the work waits, and when there’s no event, it never starts. Scheduled automations give routine work a dependable rhythm.You can already run event-based automations in GitLab Duo Agent Platform, triggered by activities like a merge request or a mention in a comment. Scheduled automations start the work on a recurring schedule, with no event needed. Describe the task in plain language, set the cadence once, and the automation runs on its own at the times you choose, with run counts and success rates your team can review.Triage new issues daily to keep your backlog organized, or schedule a flow to check CI health incidents every hour and comment with the likely root cause, so the investigation is underway before anyone opens the issue.You can set a schedule from every 15 minutes to every month, at the time of day and in the timezone that meets the needs of your group. Without a verifiable identity and a record of every change, no one can say which agent made a change or why it ran, and every review or audit starts with reconstruction. It’s hard to scale agentic work when you can’t see what agents or flows already did.Scheduled automations offer the controls a team needs to trust what runs on its own. Each automation runs as a dedicated service account with scoped permissions, so your team can tell agent work from human work in the audit events. Audit events also record changes to every automation, so your team knows what ran, what happened, and who changed it.A redesigned Automations page, previously labeled Triggers, brings scheduled and event-based automations together in one place, with run volume, success rate, and session details for each, so your team can see details of what ran and what happened. title: [Engineering at Meta] Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon
summary: Meta’s Reality Labs builds products such as AI glasses. Emulators provide us with a way to scale development and testing without relying on scarce physical hardware. Testing software for non-phone Android devices depends on how closely a virtual device reproduces the software behavior of the physical product. While a lightweight emulator like Goldfish gets you part of the way, differences from the real device can hide bugs until later in development. This lack of fidelity also erodes trust in device emulation, increasing reliance on scarce physical hardware. Cuttlefish is the Android Open Source Project’s (AOSP’s) virtual-device framework for testing Android software against virtual hardware. It boots the same system images as real hardware and runs a realistic software stack against virtual hardware. This enables Cuttlefish to more closely track a physical device’s behavior than a lightweight emulator does. Unfortunately, Cuttlefish is only supported on Linux, and our application and library developers work on Macs with Apple silicon. This forced us to support Goldfish and Cuttlefish side by side. We knew if we could consolidate onto a single Cuttlefish-based platform, we could give all of our developers the benefit of the same high-fidelity virtual device. The challenge was porting the stack to make Cuttlefish run natively on macOS. The Impact of Fragmentation Maintaining dual emulator platforms imposed a heavy operational burden: It drained computing resources, created confusion for developers, and slowed down the emulator team. Every tool required support for two separate platforms, while infrastructure and engineering capacity were divided between them. Furthermore, developers had to choose an emulator target based on how they worked: Goldfish ran everywhere but had less fidelity while Cuttlefish needed Linux. The AOSP mirrors this exact divide: Goldfish targets application developers, whereas Cuttlefish serves Android platform developers. So long as we maintained that division, we would suffer the effects of fragmentation. The Stack and the macOS Gaps Cuttlefish is the orchestration layer, while the component that actually runs the guest OS is a virtual machine monitor (VMM). On Linux, Cuttlefish normally uses crosvm but previously included support for QEMU as an alternative VMM. That integration had become inactive over time. To enable native Apple silicon support on macOS, we revived QEMU support. Many of Cuttlefish’s virtual devices use vhost-user backends, separate processes that provide virtio devices to QEMU over a socket. The architecture is clean, but large parts of it were written with a hard Linux assumption. Three of those assumptions break on macOS. The vhost-user machinery is gated to Linux and won’t build or run. The Apple hypervisor imposes resource limits QEMU didn’t expect. Finally, the native display, build, and signing paths didn’t exist. We tackled all three. The Cuttlefish-on-Mac stack. Cuttlefish orchestrates virtual devices backed by QEMU. The highlighted orange blocks are the Mac-specific work: adding macOS support to vhost-user, increasing memory-region tracking slots in QEMU’s HVF backend, and using the native Cocoa display and code-signing paths. Making vhost-user Portable Beyond Linux The most structurally important changes were in QEMU’s vhost-user path. The frontends, libvhost-user, and the contrib backends such as vhost-user-blk were all gated to Linux. We relaxed those build restrictions so the vhost-user frontends and libraries can build on macOS as well as Linux. This lets Cuttlefish’s device backends hand off to QEMU on a Mac the same way they do on Linux. Without this, the higher-fidelity device model that makes Cuttlefish worth using isn’t available outside Linux. Living Within Hypervisor.framework On Apple silicon, QEMU accelerates through HVF (Hypervisor.framework) instead of KVM. QEMU’s HVF backend did not track enough memory regions for larger Cuttlefish configurations. We increased its tracking-slot count so those configurations could run correctly. A Usable Native Display Local application development requires an interactive display allowing developers to view and engage directly with the virtual device. To enable direct interaction and bypass reliance on the WebRTC interface, we transitioned to QEMU’s native Cocoa display. The changes include: BGRA Pixel Format Support: Enables accurate display rendering to eliminate visual artifacts on Apple silicon. Mouse-Click-as-Touch: Translates pointer actions into touch input for interacting with touchscreen devices. Custom Geometry Options: Adds the -g flag to graphic_console_init for display configuration. We also enabled the unstable Rutabaga structs needed to match the Rust-side graphics ABI in gfxstream/rutabaga configurations. Building and Signing on Apple Silicon Finally, there was the build and packaging work: initial Darwin build support, building QEMU for arm64 on macOS, and toolchain fixes. The macOS builds also needed the JIT entitlement in addition to support for code signing and notarization. On the Cuttlefish side, we added macOS host support so the framework’s orchestration builds and runs on a Mac instead of assuming a Linux host. The Benefits By moving to a unified platform, we cut maintenance requirements, reduced infrastructure needs, eliminated redundant tooling, enhanced fidelity, and ensured developers run the exact same Cuttlefish virtual devices used across CI. A single platform also made it easier to support capabilities on a shared stack, including: Bluetooth pairing and connectivity. Wi-Fi. Cellular. 3D graphics. Over-the-air (OTA) update testing to exercise over-the-air update flows against a virtual device. Fastboot. Snapshotting to save and restore device state in CI and development flows. Beyond supporting Reality Labs engineers, this identical virtual device is shared with external developers building for our ecosystem. This alignment guarantees that third-party teams test against the exact same Cuttlefish-based platform we use to develop and validate the OS itself. With AI agents playing a growing role in Android development, validation execution and runtime behavior is just as essential as code generation. Virtual devices empower both engineers and automated agents to operate concurrently within isolated environments, facilitating application execution and rapid iteration. By enabling instant state resets and repeated test runs, teams eliminate dependencies on shared physical hardware and prevent workflow interruptions. Ultimately, high-fidelity emulation ensures these continuous feedback loops are both rapid and meaningful. Giving Back to the Community Although we built this for development within Reality Labs, the macOS support is useful beyond our products. We’re sharing our work with the community so other developers can build on the QEMU and AOSP foundations that enabled our work. We’re distributing the work in two parts: qemu-wearables: a Meta-maintained fork of QEMU carrying our commits. cuttlefish-wearables: a set of patch files, with instructions for patching Android/AOSP. The repositories contain our QEMU changes and the Cuttlefish patch series, along with build and patch-application instructions. We’re also exploring ways to contribute these changes upstream to QEMU and AOSP. In the meantime, developers can use our fork and patch set. Acknowledgements This project relies on the foundations laid by the QEMU and Cuttlefish/AOSP communities. We are particularly grateful for the vsock-user implementation created by Stefano Garzarella, which directly enabled our macOS integration. Special thanks also go to Olya Arkhangelskaia and Tom Care at Meta for their foundational work bringing Cuttlefish to macOS, and to Jeffrey Effendy for improvements to the native Mac developer experience and subsequent productization work. title: [Amazon AWS] AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Nitro Sandboxes, AWS Emulator, and more (November 16, 2026)
summary: A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo. I like tools that make those cases easier to investigate while a change is still small. Last week’s launch of AWS Emulator brings part of that work onto your own machine: developers and coding agents can exercise AWS API interactions, inspect results, and try again without provisioning cloud resources for every attempt. I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition. There are also new ways to isolate workloads on shared infrastructure, give an agent narrowly scoped access to a backend, and prepare search applications for a regional disruption. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools. Image: AWS. Headlines Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator introduces a generally available local environment for AWS API interactions. Point the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs at its HTTPS endpoint, and your application keeps its normal SDK calls. The walkthrough shows a coding agent creating an Amazon DynamoDB table, writing an item, and reading it back. You don’t need an AWS account for emulated operations, and there is no additional service fee. The getting-started guide covers Linux packages, Docker for macOS and Windows, and agent-assisted setup; the source is on GitHub. What I like is giving an agent concrete feedback while it works: run calls, inspect results, and revise the code. Matt Wood’s perspective on feedback for coding agents explores why that loop matters. Check the published fidelity results for your operations, because coverage varies and unimplemented calls return HTTP 501. The emulator doesn’t reproduce IAM and resource-policy enforcement or cross-account and cross-Region behavior, so test the complete application and its security configuration on AWS before production. AWS Nitro Sandboxes bring hardware isolation to pods, tasks, and VMs. You can give an Amazon EKS pod or Amazon ECS task its own VM boundary while sharing an Amazon EC2 instance. That is useful for tenant workloads, build jobs, and agents executing generated code. Isolated mode separates workloads from their neighbors; confidential mode adds protection from node operators and cryptographic attestation. The Compute Blog deep dive explains both modes and their integrations. Nitro Sandboxes have no additional charge on supported instances; EC2 and applicable EKS Auto Mode or ECS Managed Instances fees still apply. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: Amazon Cognito supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange – You can now exchange a user’s token for one scoped to a downstream service in Amazon Cognito. The derived token can have narrower permissions and a single audience, with no refresh token; supplying an actor token also identifies the intermediary in an act claim. For an agent calling a backend on someone’s behalf, that makes delegation more explicit without forwarding the original token. The feature is available on Essentials and Plus plans in all Cognito Regions. Claude Fable 5.2 is available on AWS – You can access the model through Amazon Bedrock or Claude Platform on AWS. Anthropic positions it as its most capable generally available model for technical work, including extended engineering tasks, scientific research, and quantitative finance. Bedrock has model-specific retention requirements: Fable 5.2 traffic is retained for up to 30 days for abuse detection, with a temporary zero-retention exception for eligible internal use. Amazon ElastiCache Serverless adds search and aggregations – You can now combine vector, full-text, and hybrid search with server-side aggregations in Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey. That gives product discovery, recommendations, and agent-memory retrieval another option for querying frequently changing data. The capability requires Valkey 9, so create a compatible cache or upgrade an existing one. It is available in commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US), and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. Amazon OpenSearch Service adds managed cross-Region disaster recovery – You can now pair Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running version 3.7 or later in two Regions within one account. AWS specifies recovery objectives under one minute for data loss and under 20 minutes for recovery time. Planned switchovers preserve all writes; unplanned failovers can lose unreplicated data. The deep dive covers the remaining work: keeping configuration aligned and redirecting application writes after switching roles, plus secondary-domain and data-transfer charges. Amazon CloudWatch Logs adds account-level retention policies – You can now set retention across all log groups or groups matching a name prefix in Amazon CloudWatch, with policies covering existing groups or only new ones. When policies overlap, the longest retention period applies. A platform team can set a baseline and retain security logs longer without updating every group individually. The feature has no additional charge and is available in commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE). The next generation AgentCore runtime is now the default – New Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtimes now use the next-generation runtime by default, so agent sessions start in under 2 seconds, scale up to 8 vCPU and 32 GB, scale to zero when idle, and bill up to 68% less memory, while each session still runs in its own isolated microVM. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock – This guide follows an agent’s cost through repeated calls, reasoning, caching, and human review. I like its emphasis on measuring a completed task and comparing outcomes against a documented baseline. Its worked prices are illustrative; use your own workload and reconcile estimated costs with billing data. How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions – Zillow describes reusable content modules and configuration-driven AWS Step Functions Express Workflows for more than 100 million daily notifications. The useful engineering details include idempotent modules, batching, campaign isolation, and testing expressions with the TestState API before deployment. Those patterns apply well beyond notification systems. title: [Amazon AWS] AWS Weekly Roundup: AgentCore Runtime V2, Amazon DynamoDB bulk put items, and more (November 9, 2026)
summary: Most of the cost of adopting something new isn’t the new thing, it’s the move. Moving a Hive table to Apache Iceberg has typically meant weeks of engineering work. Last week, Amazon S3 Tables turned that into three steps: start, sync as often as you need, complete. The source stays writable except for a few minutes at cutover. The same week, Amazon DynamoDB started loading data from S3 into tables that already exist. The pattern I like is that neither one asks you to stop what’s running. That’s also the way to read the agent news this week. The new Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime is a single field on the runtime you already have, and Web Answer is a tool you attach to a gateway you already run. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… Headlines The new AgentCore Runtime: elastic, optimized, and consistently fast starts – If you run agents on AgentCore and haven’t tried the new runtime since it became generally available, it’s worth a look. It changes two things. First, memory: sessions start small, page in more on demand, and give memory back when it goes cold instead of holding the peak, so you pay for what your agent uses. Second, cold starts: AgentCore prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores the snapshot for every new instance. In the team’s tests, that kept P75 cold starts at about 2 seconds for images from 200 MB up to 2 GB, while the original runtime rose from roughly 5.4 seconds to nearly 30 seconds as images grew. The per-unit rate is higher, but you use far fewer GB-hours, so the team expects most agents to see a lower bill, though that isn’t guaranteed. To opt in, you set platformVersion to V2 when you create or update a runtime. Create and update take several minutes while the snapshot is prepared, and your container must report healthy on /ping within 120 seconds, so report health only after initialization finishes. The docs cover how to optimize your agent for V2. V2 is available in 10 Regions, and committed baseline pricing is coming soon. Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg – You can now migrate Parquet tables registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog into S3 Tables without building a pipeline or provisioning compute. S3 Tables validates the source and produces a compatibility report covering every object in scope. Each sync copies only what changed, so production keeps writing until cutover. Afterward you can query the table with Amazon Athena, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, or any engine that speaks the Iceberg REST API. You pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the conversion, and objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering keep their tier. At launch it works within the same account and Region, in 10 Regions. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: Amazon DynamoDB now supports bulk put items – You can now load line-delimited DynamoDB JSON or Amazon Ion files from Amazon S3 into existing tables as a managed, asynchronous job. Each record can carry its own condition expression, so one file can mix plain, insert-only, and version-guarded writes. Writes use dedicated system capacity and cost less than the equivalent per-request writes. An Accelerated tier handles deadline-bound jobs. The Database blog post gives illustrative Accelerated times of less than 1 hour for 100 million 1 KB items. One thing to know before you start: canceling doesn’t roll back items already written. Announcing Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – You can now give an agent a single tool call that returns a synthesized, cited answer to a natural-language question, instead of building your own search, retrieval, and citation pipeline. Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, and decides when it has enough evidence. You attach it as a target on AgentCore Gateway and call it over MCP, and you can limit it with domain include and deny lists and publish-date filters. It’s available in US East (N. Virginia). The getting started post explains when to use it instead of Web Search, which returns ranked results for your own model to synthesize. AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources – You can now process records from a single Kafka partition across many parallel AWS Lambda invocations. Classic consumer groups cap parallelism at the partition count. Queue mode uses Kafka share groups and needs Kafka 4.2 or later with share groups enabled. It works with self-managed clusters and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud. You give up ordering and get at-least-once delivery, so your functions need to be idempotent. The Compute blog walkthrough covers poller scaling and when to keep stream mode. AWS announces AWS Interconnect – last mile preview with Equinix – You can now set up a private, managed connection from Equinix’s network of 282 data centers to AWS without ordering cross-connects or configuring routers. Capacity is quad-redundant across two locations and four links, with BGP and VLANs configured for you, a 99.99% availability SLA, and MACsec by default. You pick a Region, bandwidth, and AWS Direct Connect gateway, then paste the activation key into Equinix Fabric. The preview covers the San Jose metro and, as of last Thursday, Northern Virginia, with 1 Gbps connections at no charge. AWS Security Hub now provides an SBOM inventory for your compute resources – You can now see every software package installed across your organization’s Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon ECR images, and Lambda functions in AWS Security Hub, with each package’s version and how many resources run it. That’s the list you want the next time a widely used library has a vulnerability. The inventory builds on the SBOMs that Amazon Inspector already generates, so it fills in automatically wherever Inspector is enabled. It’s included in Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: Serverless ICYMI Q3 2026 – Julian Wood’s quarterly recap is a quick serverless catch-up before re:Invent: Lambda SnapStart for container images, a 90-minute timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, Lambda MicroVMs in 10 Regions, 1 MiB payloads in Amazon SNS, and the new AgentCore Runtime. AWS contributes a large-transaction binary log optimization to MySQL – With binlog on, a huge transaction holds a global commit lock while its events are copied, blocking every other commit. The optimization, which Amazon Aurora MySQL has run in production since 2019, promotes the spill file into the binlog instead of copying it. In AWS’s tests, commit latency for a 50 GiB transaction dropped from about 7 minutes to about 2 to 2.5 seconds. It has now shipped to community MySQL. How OrderServ achieved up to 64% cost savings with multi-tenant ECS – Cognizant’s food-ordering platform went from one Amazon ECS cluster per brand on AWS Fargate to a shared cluster on EC2 Auto Scaling groups with warm pools. The 64% applies to a 3-year Compute Savings Plan (47% with a 1-year plan). Scaling time also fell from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds.
